notes.body:
The musculoskeletal system depends on living tissues that constantly remodel in response to load and hormones. Understanding their structure explains most MSK disease.

Bone
- Matrix: about one-third organic (mostly type I collagen, giving tensile strength and flexibility) and two-thirds mineral (hydroxyapatite, giving compressive strength).
- Cortical (compact) bone forms shafts and is organised into osteons (Haversian systems); trabecular (cancellous) bone fills metaphyses and vertebral bodies, has a large surface area and turns over faster, so it is lost first in osteoporosis.
- Cells: osteoblasts (from mesenchymal stem cells) lay down osteoid and mineralise it; osteocytes are buried osteoblasts that sense mechanical strain and secrete sclerostin and FGF23; osteoclasts (from the monocyte–macrophage lineage) resorb bone.
- Coupling: osteoblasts express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive their formation; osteoprotegerin (OPG) is a decoy receptor that blocks this. Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL.
- Wolff's law: bone adapts its architecture to the loads placed on it.

Calcium and phosphate regulation
- PTH raises serum calcium by increasing bone resorption (indirectly, via osteoblast RANKL), distal tubular calcium reabsorption and renal 1α-hydroxylation of vitamin D; it also increases phosphate excretion.
- Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption. FGF23 promotes phosphate excretion and suppresses calcitriol.

Growth
- Long bones form by endochondral ossification on a cartilage model; flat skull bones by intramembranous ossification. The growth plate has resting, proliferative, hypertrophic and calcification zones. Achondroplasia results from activating FGFR3 mutations.

Joints and connective tissue
- Synovial joints have hyaline articular cartilage: avascular, with chondrocytes in a matrix of type II collagen and aggrecan, whose negatively charged glycosaminoglycans hold water and resist compression. Synovial fluid contains hyaluronan and lubricin. Tendons and ligaments are mainly type I collagen.

Skeletal muscle
- Excitation–contraction coupling: an action potential travels down T-tubules; dihydropyridine receptors sense voltage and open ryanodine receptors (RyR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum; Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, tropomyosin shifts and myosin cross-bridges cycle. ATP is required for detachment (hence rigor mortis) and for SERCA to pump Ca²⁺ back.
- Type I fibres are slow and oxidative (posture, endurance); type II fibres are fast and more glycolytic (power).

Applied illustration
Bone biochemistry distinguishes metabolic bone diseases:
- Osteoporosis: calcium, phosphate and ALP normal.
- Osteomalacia: calcium low or normal, phosphate low, ALP and PTH raised.
- Paget's disease: isolated raised ALP.
- Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low phosphate, PTH inappropriately normal or high.

Exam pitfalls
- Osteoporosis is reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation; osteomalacia is defective mineralisation.
- Stopping denosumab causes rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures unless followed by another treatment, usually a bisphosphonate.

A fracture is a break in the structural continuity of bone. Its description, mechanism and soft-tissue injury determine management and prognosis.

Describing a fracture
- Open or closed; bone and location (diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis, intra-articular); pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, avulsion); displacement (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening).
- Special types: pathological (through abnormal bone, e.g. metastasis or osteoporosis), stress (repetitive loading), greenstick and buckle (children).
- Salter–Harris classification of physeal injuries (types I–V): type II, through the physis and metaphysis, is commonest; types III–V carry greater risk of growth disturbance.
- Gustilo–Anderson classification of open fractures: I (small clean wound), II (moderate), III (extensive soft-tissue damage; IIIA adequate cover, IIIB needs flap cover, IIIC arterial injury requiring repair).

Healing
- Secondary (indirect) healing via callus occurs with relative stability (casts, intramedullary nails, external fixators): haematoma and inflammation, soft callus (cartilage), hard callus (woven bone), then remodelling into lamellar bone over months to years.
- Primary (direct) healing without callus occurs with absolute stability and anatomical reduction (compression plating, lag screws): cutting cones of osteoclasts and osteoblasts cross the fracture.
- Perren's strain theory: bone forms only when interfragmentary strain is low; very low strain allows direct healing, moderate strain produces callus, high strain causes non-union.
- Impaired healing: smoking, diabetes, poor blood supply, infection, excessive movement, malnutrition and corticosteroids.

Principles and complications
- Resuscitate (ATLS), then reduce, hold and rehabilitate.
- Early: compartment syndrome, neurovascular injury, fat embolism (respiratory distress, confusion, petechial rash), VTE, infection.
- Late: malunion, non-union, avascular necrosis (scaphoid, intracapsular femoral neck, talus), post-traumatic arthritis, complex regional pain syndrome.
- Open fractures (BOAST 2017; NICE NG37): intravenous antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within an hour of injury; photograph and cover the wound; tetanus status; early debridement by combined orthopaedic–plastic teams.
- Hip fracture (NICE CG124): surgery on the day of, or day after, admission. Displaced intracapsular fractures are treated with arthroplasty (total hip replacement for suitable, independently mobile patients); extracapsular trochanteric fractures with a sliding hip screw, or an intramedullary nail for subtrochanteric fractures.

Worked example
A man with a tibial shaft fracture has escalating pain despite analgesia and pain on passive toe flexion. His diastolic pressure is 70 mmHg and anterior compartment pressure 45 mmHg. Delta pressure = 70 − 45 = 25 mmHg; below 30 mmHg supports compartment syndrome, so he needs urgent fasciotomy.

Exam pitfalls
- Palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome; pain out of proportion is the earliest sign.
- Scaphoid fractures may be invisible on initial radiographs; treat clinical suspicion and image further.
- Intracapsular hip fractures threaten the femoral head blood supply, which is why displaced ones are replaced rather than fixed.

Arthritis is classified as degenerative, inflammatory, crystal or infective. Pattern, morning stiffness and systemic features point to the category.

Osteoarthritis (OA)
- Cartilage loss with subchondral bone remodelling. X-ray: loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts. Heberden's (DIP) and Bouchard's (PIP) nodes; first CMC joint, knees and hips commonly affected.
- NICE NG226 (2022): diagnose clinically without imaging if aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting 30 minutes or less. Core treatment is exercise, weight loss if needed and education. Offer topical NSAIDs for knee OA; oral NSAIDs for the shortest time with gastroprotection. Do not routinely offer paracetamol or weak opioids, and do not offer glucosamine or strong opioids. Joint replacement for severe symptoms.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
- Autoimmune synovitis with erosive pannus: symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis, morning stiffness over an hour, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP (more specific). Extra-articular disease includes nodules, interstitial lung disease, scleritis and accelerated cardiovascular disease.
- 2010 ACR/EULAR classification: a score of 6 or more out of 10 (joints, serology, acute-phase reactants, duration).
- NICE NG100: start conventional DMARD monotherapy (methotrexate, leflunomide or sulfasalazine) as soon as possible, ideally within 3 months of persistent symptoms; hydroxychloroquine for mild disease; short-term glucocorticoid bridging; treat to target (remission or low disease activity on DAS28). Biologics (TNF inhibitors, abatacept, tocilizumab, rituximab) and JAK inhibitors are used for active disease despite conventional DMARDs; the MHRA (2023) advises JAK inhibitors in over-65s, long-term smokers or those at raised cardiovascular or cancer risk only if no suitable alternative exists.

Spondyloarthritis
- HLA-B27-associated: axial spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis (dactylitis, nail pitting, DIP disease), reactive and enteropathic arthritis. Inflammatory back pain improves with exercise. NSAIDs first line, then TNF or IL-17 inhibitors.

Crystal arthritis
- Gout: monosodium urate crystals, needle-shaped and negatively birefringent. NICE NG219 (2022): treat flares with an NSAID, colchicine or a corticosteroid; offer urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol or febuxostat) using treat-to-target, aiming for serum urate below 360 µmol/L (below 300 µmol/L with tophi or ongoing flares), with colchicine cover while starting.
- CPPD (pseudogout): rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals; chondrocalcinosis on X-ray.

Septic arthritis
- An emergency, most often Staphylococcus aureus (gonococcus in young sexually active adults). Aspirate and take blood cultures before antibiotics where this causes no delay; arrange washout.

Worked example
A 52-year-old woman has 6 weeks of swelling in 6 small hand joints, strongly positive anti-CCP and raised CRP. Score: joints 3 + serology 3 + acute-phase 1 + duration 1 = 8, so she meets classification criteria for RA.

Exam pitfalls
- A hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise, even in known gout.
- Serum urate can be normal during a gout flare.

MSK examination follows a structured routine: screen, then examine the relevant region by look, feel, move and special tests, then assess the joints above and below and neurovascular status.

GALS screen (Doherty and colleagues, 1992)
- Three screening questions: any pain or stiffness in muscles, joints or back; can you dress completely without difficulty; can you manage stairs without difficulty.
- Gait, Arms, Legs, Spine: inspect symmetry and smoothness of gait, then quick functional tests such as the metacarpophalangeal squeeze test (tender in early inflammatory arthritis), power and precision grips, and lumbar flexion.

Regional examination (REMS)
- Look: scars, swelling, wasting, deformity, skin changes (psoriasis, rheumatoid nodules), posture.
- Feel: temperature, tenderness, effusion, crepitus.
- Move: active then passive range; loss of passive as well as active movement suggests intra-articular or capsular pathology, while preserved passive with lost active movement suggests tendon or nerve problems.

Key special tests
- Shoulder: painful arc (subacromial impingement); Jobe's empty-can test (supraspinatus); resisted external rotation (infraspinatus, teres minor); Gerber lift-off (subscapularis); global loss of passive external rotation suggests adhesive capsulitis.
- Hand and wrist: Phalen's and Tinel's tests (carpal tunnel); Finkelstein's test (de Quervain's tenosynovitis); Froment's sign (ulnar nerve, adductor pollicis weakness).
- Hip: Thomas test (fixed flexion deformity); Trendelenburg test (abductor weakness or superior gluteal nerve lesion).
- Knee: patellar tap and sweep test (effusion); Lachman and anterior drawer (ACL); posterior sag (PCL); valgus and varus stress (collateral ligaments); McMurray's test (meniscus).
- Spine: modified Schober's test (reduced lumbar flexion in axial spondyloarthritis); straight leg raise (L4–S1 root tension); femoral stretch test (L2–L4).

Neurological correlation
- Myotomes: L2 hip flexion, L3 knee extension, L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 great toe extension, S1 plantarflexion.
- Reflexes: biceps C5–6, triceps C7, knee L3–4, ankle S1.

Red flags in back pain
- Cauda equina syndrome (saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica, sexual dysfunction) needs emergency MRI. Also consider malignancy (history of cancer, weight loss, night pain), infection (fever, immunosuppression, IV drug use) and fracture (trauma, osteoporosis, steroids). NICE NG59 advises against routine imaging for non-specific low back pain.

Worked example
Standing on her right leg, a woman's left hemipelvis drops. This is a positive Trendelenburg test on the right: the right hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) cannot stabilise the pelvis, from weakness, pain, a superior gluteal nerve lesion or hip pathology.

Exam pitfalls
- In the Trendelenburg test the pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak abductors.
- Always expose and compare both sides, and examine the joint above and below.
- Ottawa ankle rules decide X-ray by bony tenderness at the malleoli or inability to bear weight, not by swelling.

Haematopoiesis is the production of all blood cells from a small population of self-renewing haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).

Sites
- Yolk sac, then liver and spleen, then bone marrow from late fetal life; in adults mainly the axial skeleton and proximal long bones. Extramedullary haematopoiesis can recur in myelofibrosis and severe haemolysis.

Lineages and growth factors
- HSCs give rise to common myeloid progenitors (red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes) and common lymphoid progenitors (B, T and NK cells).
- Erythropoietin is made by peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex in response to hypoxia, sensed through hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). Thrombopoietin comes mainly from the liver. G-CSF drives neutrophil production and is used to shorten neutropenia.

Red cells
- Biconcave, anucleate, flexible; lifespan about 120 days, then removed by splenic macrophages. Haem is broken down to unconjugated bilirubin.
- Adult haemoglobin: HbA (α2β2) predominates, with small amounts of HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2).
- The oxygen dissociation curve is shifted right (easier unloading) by raised CO2, H⁺ (Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG. HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its curve lies to the left, favouring transfer from mother to fetus.
- Reticulocytes are young red cells with residual RNA; their count reflects marrow output.

White cells and platelets
- Neutrophils (phagocytosis, the first responders), eosinophils (parasites, allergy), basophils (histamine), monocytes (become tissue macrophages) and lymphocytes (adaptive immunity).
- Platelets are fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm and survive about 7–10 days.

Haematinics
- Iron is absorbed in the duodenum via DMT1 and exported by ferroportin. Hepcidin, made by the liver, degrades ferroportin: it rises in inflammation (trapping iron in macrophages) and falls in iron deficiency. HFE haemochromatosis causes inappropriately low hepcidin.
- Ferritin reflects iron stores but rises as an acute-phase reactant.
- Vitamin B12 binds haptocorrin in the stomach, then intrinsic factor (from parietal cells) in the duodenum, and is absorbed in the terminal ileum. Folate is absorbed in the proximal small bowel.

Blood film terms
- Target cells (liver disease, thalassaemia, hyposplenism), Howell–Jolly bodies (hyposplenism), spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis, warm AIHA), schistocytes (microangiopathic haemolysis), bite cells and Heinz bodies (G6PD deficiency), teardrop cells (marrow fibrosis), hypersegmented neutrophils (megaloblastic anaemia).

Worked example
Red cell indices are derived: MCV = haematocrit ÷ red cell count. With haematocrit 0.36 and red cell count 4.0 × 10¹²/L, MCV = 0.36 ÷ (4.0 × 10¹²) L = 90 × 10⁻¹⁵ L = 90 fL (normocytic). MCH = Hb ÷ red cell count = 120 g/L ÷ (4.0 × 10¹²/L) = 30 pg.

Exam pitfalls
- A normal ferritin does not exclude iron deficiency during inflammation.
- A high reticulocyte count raises the MCV, because reticulocytes are larger than mature red cells.

Anaemia is a haemoglobin concentration below the reference range (WHO thresholds: below 130 g/L in adult men and 120 g/L in non-pregnant women). Classifying it by MCV and reticulocyte response guides investigation.

Microcytic anaemia
- Iron deficiency: low ferritin, raised transferrin/TIBC, pencil cells. Always find the cause: menstrual loss, GI blood loss (including colorectal cancer), malabsorption (coeliac disease) or poor intake. The British Society of Gastroenterology guideline (2021) recommends coeliac serology for all and bidirectional endoscopy for men and postmenopausal women unless another cause is clear. Oral iron is first line; intravenous iron if oral is ineffective or not tolerated.
- Thalassaemia trait: microcytosis out of proportion to the anaemia with a high red cell count; β-thalassaemia trait shows raised HbA2.
- Anaemia of chronic disease (often normocytic) and sideroblastic anaemia.

Normocytic anaemia
- Acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease (hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration), CKD (reduced erythropoietin; treated with ESAs once iron replete), marrow infiltration or failure, and early haemolysis.

Macrocytic anaemia
- Megaloblastic: B12 or folate deficiency, or drugs impairing DNA synthesis (methotrexate, hydroxycarbamide). Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune gastritis) is autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor; anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are specific but a negative result does not exclude it, and anti-parietal cell antibodies are sensitive but non-specific. NICE NG239 (2024) advises testing anti-intrinsic factor antibodies first, adding parietal cell antibodies only if suspicion remains, and lifelong intramuscular B12 when autoimmune gastritis is the cause. B12 deficiency can cause subacute combined degeneration of the cord; replace B12 before folate.
- Non-megaloblastic: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, myelodysplasia, pregnancy.

Haemolytic anaemia
- Laboratory features: raised reticulocytes, unconjugated bilirubin and LDH; low haptoglobin.
- Inherited: membrane defects (hereditary spherocytosis: spherocytes, splenomegaly, gallstones; EMA binding test), enzyme defects (G6PD deficiency: X-linked, oxidant triggers such as fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin; bite cells and Heinz bodies) and haemoglobinopathies.
- Acquired: warm (IgG) or cold (IgM) autoimmune haemolysis (direct antiglobulin test positive), microangiopathic haemolysis (TTP, HUS, DIC), infection such as malaria, and PNH.

Haemoglobinopathies
- Sickle cell disease: HbS (β-globin Glu6Val) polymerises when deoxygenated, causing vaso-occlusive pain, acute chest syndrome, stroke, splenic sequestration, aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19) and functional hyposplenism (vaccination and penicillin prophylaxis). Hydroxycarbamide raises HbF. NICE CG143 advises analgesia within 30 minutes for acute painful crises.
- Thalassaemias reduce globin chain synthesis. α: HbH disease (three genes deleted), Hb Barts hydrops fetalis (four). β-thalassaemia major needs regular transfusion with iron chelation (desferrioxamine, deferasirox, deferiprone).

Worked example
The Mentzer index (MCV ÷ red cell count in 10¹²/L) helps separate microcytic causes. MCV 64 fL with red cells 5.8 gives 11.0 (below 13, suggesting thalassaemia trait). MCV 70 fL with red cells 4.0 gives 17.5 (above 13, suggesting iron deficiency). Confirm with ferritin and haemoglobin analysis.

Exam pitfalls
- G6PD levels can be falsely normal during acute haemolysis, because young cells have more enzyme; retest after recovery.
- Do not give folate alone to a patient who may be B12 deficient.

Haemostasis balances clot formation against fibrinolysis. Bleeding patterns and coagulation tests localise the defect.

Primary haemostasis
- Platelets adhere to exposed collagen via von Willebrand factor (vWF) binding GPIb, release ADP and thromboxane A2, and aggregate through GPIIb/IIIa binding fibrinogen.
- Defects (thrombocytopenia, platelet dysfunction, von Willebrand disease) cause mucocutaneous bleeding: petechiae, epistaxis, menorrhagia.

Secondary haemostasis
- Cell-based model: tissue factor–factor VIIa initiates a small amount of thrombin on TF-bearing cells; thrombin amplifies by activating platelets and factors V, VIII and XI; on the platelet surface, tenase (IXa–VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa–Va) produce a thrombin burst that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, cross-linked by factor XIIIa.
- Defects cause deep bleeding: haemarthroses, muscle haematomas and delayed bleeding after surgery.
- Natural anticoagulants: antithrombin, proteins C and S, TFPI. Plasmin (activated by tPA) degrades fibrin to D-dimers.

Coagulation tests
- PT (INR) tests factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen: prolonged by warfarin, vitamin K deficiency and liver disease.
- APTT tests XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen: prolonged by haemophilia, heparin and lupus anticoagulant.
- Mixing study: correction with normal plasma suggests factor deficiency; failure suggests an inhibitor.

Inherited bleeding disorders
- Haemophilia A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX) are X-linked recessive, so affected individuals are mostly male. Severity follows factor activity (severe below 1%). Treatment: factor concentrates, emicizumab (a bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIIIa by bridging IXa and X) for haemophilia A, and gene therapy in selected patients; desmopressin in mild haemophilia A.
- Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, usually autosomal dominant type 1 (partial quantitative deficiency). Type 2 is qualitative and type 3 severe. Treatments include desmopressin, tranexamic acid and vWF-containing concentrate.

Acquired disorders
- ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia, a diagnosis of exclusion; steroids, IVIG, thrombopoietin receptor agonists.
- TTP: severe ADAMTS13 deficiency leaves ultra-large vWF multimers, causing microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and organ ischaemia. Urgent plasma exchange with immunosuppression, often with caplacizumab.
- DIC: consumption of platelets and factors, giving low platelets and fibrinogen, prolonged PT and APTT and raised D-dimer. Treat the cause.
- Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: antibodies to PF4–heparin activate platelets, causing thrombosis typically 5–10 days after starting heparin. Stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant.

Worked example
A 3-year-old boy has a swollen, painful knee after a minor fall. PT is normal, APTT prolonged and corrects on mixing, platelets normal. This points to deficiency of factor VIII, IX or XI; in a boy with haemarthrosis, haemophilia A or B is most likely, confirmed by factor assays.

Exam pitfalls
- Factor XII deficiency prolongs APTT without causing bleeding.
- Lupus anticoagulant prolongs APTT yet predisposes to thrombosis.
- Avoid platelet transfusion in TTP and HIT unless bleeding is life-threatening.

Haematological malignancies are clonal disorders classified by lineage, maturity and genetics (WHO 5th edition and International Consensus Classification, 2022).

Acute leukaemias
- Blasts accumulate, causing marrow failure: anaemia, infection, bleeding.
- Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), mainly in older adults: myeloblasts, sometimes with Auer rods. Diagnosis usually needs at least 20% blasts in blood or marrow, but defining genetic abnormalities allow diagnosis at lower counts.
- Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (PML::RARA, t(15;17)) presents with DIC and is an emergency; all-trans retinoic acid with arsenic trioxide is highly effective.
- Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the commonest childhood cancer; it can involve the CNS and testes. Most children are cured.

Chronic leukaemias
- Chronic myeloid leukaemia: the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creates the BCR::ABL1 tyrosine kinase. Features: raised granulocytes at all stages of maturation, basophilia and marked splenomegaly. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib and successors) transformed survival.
- Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL): commonest adult leukaemia in the UK; CD5+, CD19+, CD23+ B cells, smudge cells on film. Often monitored without treatment. Complications: autoimmune cytopenias, hypogammaglobulinaemia with infections, Richter transformation. Active disease is treated with BTK inhibitors or venetoclax-based regimens; TP53 disruption predicts poor response to chemoimmunotherapy.

Lymphomas
- Hodgkin lymphoma: Reed–Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+); bimodal age distribution; EBV association; contiguous nodal spread. B symptoms (fevers, night sweats, weight loss over 10% in 6 months) worsen prognosis. Lugano staging with PET-CT.
- Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the commonest (aggressive, treated with rituximab-containing chemotherapy); follicular lymphoma t(14;18) with BCL2 overexpression (indolent); Burkitt lymphoma t(8;14) with MYC ("starry sky"); mantle cell t(11;14) with cyclin D1; gastric MALT lymphoma associated with Helicobacter pylori.

Plasma cell disorders
- Myeloma (IMWG 2014): clonal marrow plasma cells of at least 10% (or a plasmacytoma) plus a myeloma-defining event, either CRAB (hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, lytic bone lesions) or a SLiM biomarker (60% or more clonal plasma cells, involved:uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or more, or more than one focal MRI lesion). 
- MGUS is a precursor without end-organ damage (progression roughly 1% per year).

Myeloproliferative neoplasms and MDS
- Polycythaemia vera (JAK2 mutations in almost all cases), essential thrombocythaemia (JAK2, CALR or MPL), primary myelofibrosis (teardrop cells). Myelodysplastic syndromes cause dysplastic cytopenias and may progress to AML.

Emergencies
- Neutropenic sepsis: immediate empirical piperacillin with tazobactam (NICE CG151), without waiting for the neutrophil count.
- Tumour lysis syndrome: hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia and AKI. Prevent with hydration and allopurinol or rasburicase.

Applied illustration
An older patient with back pain, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment and anaemia needs serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains to look for myeloma.

Exam pitfalls
- Light-chain myeloma may lack a serum paraprotein band; request free light chains.
- Avoid rasburicase in G6PD deficiency.

cards.f: What are the organic and mineral components of bone matrix, and what does each contribute?
cards.b: The organic component is mainly type I collagen, which gives tensile strength and flexibility. The mineral component is hydroxyapatite, which gives compressive strength and stiffness.

cards.f: Name the three main bone cell types and their roles.
cards.b: Osteoblasts form and mineralise osteoid; osteocytes are embedded former osteoblasts that sense strain and regulate remodelling; osteoclasts are multinucleated cells of monocyte–macrophage origin that resorb bone.

cards.f: Explain the RANK/RANKL/OPG system.
cards.b: Osteoblasts and osteocytes express RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors to drive osteoclast formation and activity. Osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that binds RANKL and limits resorption.

cards.f: How does denosumab work, and what is the risk on stopping it?
cards.b: It is a monoclonal antibody against RANKL that blocks osteoclast formation. Stopping it without follow-on therapy causes rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures, so a bisphosphonate is usually given afterwards.

cards.f: Why is trabecular bone lost earlier than cortical bone in osteoporosis?
cards.b: Trabecular bone has a much larger surface area and higher turnover, so an imbalance between resorption and formation affects it first; vertebral bodies and the distal radius are therefore early fracture sites.

cards.f: List three actions of PTH that raise serum calcium.
cards.b: Increased bone resorption (indirectly via osteoblast RANKL), increased calcium reabsorption in the distal nephron, and stimulation of renal 1α-hydroxylase to make calcitriol, which increases gut absorption.

cards.f: What does FGF23 do?
cards.b: Secreted by osteocytes, it increases renal phosphate excretion and suppresses 1α-hydroxylase, lowering calcitriol. Excess causes hypophosphataemic rickets/osteomalacia.

cards.f: Describe excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle.
cards.b: The action potential spreads down T-tubules; dihydropyridine receptors sense the voltage and open RyR1 channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Released Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, moving tropomyosin so myosin can bind actin and cycle.

cards.f: Why does rigor mortis occur?
cards.b: ATP is needed for myosin to detach from actin. After death ATP is depleted, so cross-bridges remain locked until proteins degrade.

cards.f: What gives articular cartilage its resistance to compression?
cards.b: Aggrecan's negatively charged glycosaminoglycans attract water, creating swelling pressure restrained by a type II collagen network. Cartilage is avascular and depends on diffusion from synovial fluid.

cards.f: Contrast endochondral and intramembranous ossification.
cards.b: Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model with bone (long bones, vertebrae) and continues at growth plates. Intramembranous ossification forms bone directly from mesenchyme (flat skull bones, clavicle).

cards.f: Give the typical bone biochemistry in osteomalacia.
cards.b: Low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase and raised PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), with low 25-hydroxyvitamin D when vitamin D deficiency is the cause.

cards.f: Name the four stages of secondary fracture healing.
cards.b: Haematoma and inflammation; soft (cartilaginous) callus; hard (woven bone) callus; remodelling into lamellar bone.

cards.f: Primary vs secondary bone healing?
cards.b: Primary healing occurs with absolute stability and anatomical reduction (compression plating) and proceeds without callus via cutting cones. Secondary healing occurs with relative stability (casts, nails) and proceeds through callus.

cards.f: State Perren's strain theory.
cards.b: Tissue type formed in a fracture gap depends on interfragmentary strain: very low strain allows direct bone healing, moderate strain favours callus, and high strain prevents bone formation (non-union).

cards.f: Outline the Salter–Harris classification.
cards.b: I: through the physis; II: physis and metaphysis (commonest); III: physis and epiphysis; IV: across metaphysis, physis and epiphysis; V: crush of the physis. Higher types carry more risk of growth arrest.

cards.f: What is the Gustilo–Anderson classification?
cards.b: A grading of open fractures by wound size, contamination and soft-tissue damage: I, II and III, with III subdivided into A (adequate cover), B (periosteal stripping needing flap cover) and C (arterial injury needing repair).

cards.f: What is the earliest and most reliable sign of compartment syndrome?
cards.b: Pain out of proportion to the injury, made worse by passive stretch of the muscles in the compartment. Pulselessness is a late sign and pulses are often present.

cards.f: When does compartment pressure measurement support fasciotomy?
cards.b: When the delta pressure (diastolic blood pressure minus compartment pressure) is less than 30 mmHg, in the right clinical context.

cards.f: Which fractures carry a high risk of avascular necrosis, and why?
cards.b: Scaphoid waist/proximal pole (retrograde blood supply from distal), displaced intracapsular femoral neck (disrupts retinacular vessels from the medial circumflex femoral artery) and talar neck.

cards.f: Key early steps for an open fracture?
cards.b: Intravenous antibiotics as soon as possible (ideally within an hour), tetanus prophylaxis, photograph and cover the wound with a saline-soaked dressing, splint, neurovascular checks, then early debridement by combined orthoplastic teams.

cards.f: What is the classic triad of fat embolism syndrome?
cards.b: Respiratory distress (hypoxaemia), neurological impairment (confusion) and a petechial rash, typically 24–72 hours after long-bone or pelvic fracture.

cards.f: How are displaced intracapsular and extracapsular hip fractures treated?
cards.b: Displaced intracapsular: arthroplasty (hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement in suitable patients), because the femoral head blood supply is compromised. Extracapsular trochanteric: sliding hip screw; subtrochanteric: intramedullary nail.

cards.f: List four factors that impair fracture healing.
cards.b: Smoking, diabetes, poor blood supply, infection, excessive movement at the fracture, malnutrition and corticosteroid use; any four.

cards.f: What is a pathological fracture?
cards.b: A fracture through bone weakened by disease (metastasis, myeloma, osteoporosis, Paget's disease) after trauma that would not break normal bone.

cards.f: List the four radiographic features of osteoarthritis.
cards.b: Loss of joint space (narrowing), osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and subchondral cysts.

cards.f: When can OA be diagnosed clinically without imaging (NICE NG226)?
cards.b: In people aged 45 or over with activity-related joint pain and either no morning stiffness or stiffness lasting no more than 30 minutes.

cards.f: Which is more specific for rheumatoid arthritis: rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP?
cards.b: Anti-CCP (ACPA) is highly specific and also predicts erosive disease. Rheumatoid factor is less specific, occurring in other autoimmune diseases, chronic infection and some healthy older people.

cards.f: First-line DMARD approach in newly diagnosed RA (NICE NG100)?
cards.b: Conventional DMARD monotherapy with methotrexate, leflunomide or sulfasalazine started as soon as possible, ideally within 3 months of persistent symptoms; hydroxychloroquine for mild or palindromic disease; short-term bridging steroids.

cards.f: What does 'treat to target' mean in RA?
cards.b: Escalating therapy until a predefined target of remission or low disease activity, usually measured by DAS28, is reached, with regular reassessment.

cards.f: Gout vs pseudogout crystals under polarised light?
cards.b: Gout: monosodium urate, needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent. Pseudogout: calcium pyrophosphate, rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent.

cards.f: Serum urate target on urate-lowering therapy (NICE NG219)?
cards.b: Below 360 µmol/L, or below 300 µmol/L for people with tophi, chronic gouty arthritis or continuing frequent flares.

cards.f: Why is colchicine given when starting urate-lowering therapy?
cards.b: Rapid falls in urate mobilise crystals and can trigger flares; colchicine (or an NSAID) is given as prophylaxis during the first months of treatment.

cards.f: Which features suggest inflammatory back pain?
cards.b: Onset before about 40, insidious onset, improvement with exercise but not rest, night pain (often second half of the night) and prolonged morning stiffness.

cards.f: List three features of psoriatic arthritis that distinguish it from RA.
cards.b: DIP joint involvement, dactylitis, nail pitting or onycholysis, enthesitis, asymmetrical distribution, and usually negative rheumatoid factor; arthritis mutilans in severe cases.

cards.f: What is reactive arthritis?
cards.b: A sterile inflammatory arthritis developing after infection elsewhere, typically enteric (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Yersinia) or genital (Chlamydia); may occur with urethritis and conjunctivitis; associated with HLA-B27.

cards.f: Most common organism in septic arthritis and the key first investigation?
cards.b: Staphylococcus aureus. Joint aspiration for Gram stain, culture and crystals, ideally before antibiotics, plus blood cultures.

cards.f: What MHRA advice (2023) applies to JAK inhibitors?
cards.b: In people aged 65 or over, current or past long-term smokers, and those with raised cardiovascular or malignancy risk, they should be used only when no suitable alternative exists, because of risks of major cardiovascular events, malignancy and VTE.

cards.f: What are the three GALS screening questions?
cards.b: Do you have any pain or stiffness in your muscles, joints or back? Can you dress yourself completely without any difficulty? Can you walk up and down stairs without any difficulty?

cards.f: What does a positive metatarsophalangeal or metacarpophalangeal squeeze test suggest?
cards.b: Tenderness on squeezing across the joints suggests synovitis, as in early inflammatory arthritis such as RA.

cards.f: Interpret a positive Trendelenburg test on the right.
cards.b: When standing on the right leg the left side of the pelvis drops, indicating weakness or dysfunction of the right hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) or the superior gluteal nerve, or right hip pathology.

cards.f: What does the Thomas test detect?
cards.b: A fixed flexion deformity of the hip: with the opposite hip fully flexed to flatten the lumbar lordosis, the tested thigh lifts off the couch.

cards.f: Which test is most sensitive for an ACL tear?
cards.b: Lachman's test (anterior translation of the tibia with the knee at about 20–30° flexion), assessing laxity and a soft end-point.

cards.f: Name the special tests for each rotator cuff muscle.
cards.b: Supraspinatus: Jobe's empty-can test. Infraspinatus and teres minor: resisted external rotation. Subscapularis: Gerber lift-off or belly-press test.

cards.f: Which finding suggests adhesive capsulitis rather than a rotator cuff tear?
cards.b: Global loss of both active and passive movement, especially external rotation. A cuff tear typically limits active movement with relatively preserved passive range.

cards.f: What is the modified Schober's test?
cards.b: Marks are made at the lumbosacral junction (dimples of Venus) and 10 cm above (and often 5 cm below); an increase of less than 5 cm on forward flexion suggests reduced lumbar flexion, as in axial spondyloarthritis.

cards.f: Which nerve roots does the straight leg raise test and femoral stretch test assess?
cards.b: Straight leg raise: L4–S1 (sciatic nerve roots, commonly L5/S1 disc prolapse). Femoral stretch test: L2–L4.

cards.f: Give the root value for each reflex: biceps, triceps, knee, ankle.
cards.b: Biceps C5–6; triceps C7; knee L3–4; ankle S1.

cards.f: Which myotome is tested by ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension?
cards.b: Ankle dorsiflexion is mainly L4; great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) is L5.

cards.f: Name four red flags for cauda equina syndrome.
cards.b: Saddle anaesthesia, new bladder dysfunction (retention or incontinence), bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica or leg weakness, and sexual dysfunction; needs emergency MRI.

cards.f: What do Phalen's and Tinel's tests assess?
cards.b: Carpal tunnel syndrome: Phalen's holds the wrists in full flexion to reproduce median nerve paraesthesia; Tinel's taps over the carpal tunnel to provoke tingling.

cards.f: State the Ottawa ankle rules.
cards.b: Ankle X-ray is needed if there is malleolar-zone pain and either bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and in the department.

cards.f: Where does haematopoiesis occur during development and in adults?
cards.b: Yolk sac first, then liver and spleen, then bone marrow from late fetal life. In adults it occurs mainly in the axial skeleton (vertebrae, pelvis, sternum, ribs, skull) and proximal femur and humerus.

cards.f: Where is erythropoietin produced and what stimulates it?
cards.b: By peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex, in response to reduced oxygen delivery sensed through hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF).

cards.f: List four factors that shift the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.
cards.b: Raised PCO2, raised H⁺ (lower pH; the Bohr effect), raised temperature and raised 2,3-BPG.

cards.f: Why does HbF have a higher oxygen affinity than HbA?
cards.b: Its γ chains bind 2,3-BPG poorly, so the curve shifts left, favouring oxygen transfer from maternal to fetal blood.

cards.f: What is hepcidin and how does it regulate iron?
cards.b: A liver-derived peptide that binds and degrades ferroportin, reducing iron absorption from enterocytes and release from macrophages. It rises in inflammation and falls in iron deficiency and hypoxia.

cards.f: Describe vitamin B12 absorption.
cards.b: B12 binds haptocorrin in the stomach, is released by pancreatic proteases in the duodenum, binds intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells, and is absorbed in the terminal ileum.

cards.f: What is a reticulocyte and why measure it?
cards.b: A young red cell containing residual ribosomal RNA. The reticulocyte count reflects marrow output: high in haemolysis or bleeding, low in marrow failure or haematinic deficiency.

cards.f: What do Howell–Jolly bodies indicate?
cards.b: Nuclear remnants in red cells that are normally removed by the spleen; they indicate hyposplenism or splenectomy.

cards.f: What do bite cells and Heinz bodies suggest?
cards.b: Oxidative haemolysis, classically G6PD deficiency: Heinz bodies are precipitated denatured haemoglobin, and bite cells result when the spleen removes them.

cards.f: What does the presence of schistocytes indicate?
cards.b: Fragmented red cells from mechanical damage: microangiopathic haemolysis (TTP, HUS, DIC, malignant hypertension) or mechanical heart valves.

cards.f: Calculate MCV from haematocrit 0.42 and red cell count 4.2 × 10¹²/L.
cards.b: MCV = haematocrit ÷ red cell count = 0.42 ÷ (4.2 × 10¹²/L) = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³ L = 100 fL, which is at the upper limit of normal or mildly macrocytic depending on the laboratory.

cards.f: Why can ferritin be misleading in inflammation?
cards.b: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant, so it rises with inflammation, infection, liver disease or malignancy and may be normal despite iron deficiency.

cards.f: Name the main haemoglobin types in adult blood.
cards.b: HbA (α2β2), the majority; HbA2 (α2δ2), a small fraction; and HbF (α2γ2), a trace.

cards.f: Classify anaemia by MCV with two causes each.
cards.b: Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassaemia. Normocytic: acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease or CKD. Macrocytic: B12/folate deficiency, alcohol or liver disease (also hypothyroidism, drugs).

cards.f: Which investigations does the BSG (2021) recommend for iron-deficiency anaemia in men and postmenopausal women?
cards.b: Coeliac serology and bidirectional endoscopy (gastroscopy and colonoscopy, or CT colonography if colonoscopy is unsuitable), unless another cause is clearly identified.

cards.f: Calculate the Mentzer index for MCV 62 fL and red cell count 5.6 × 10¹²/L, and interpret it.
cards.b: 62 ÷ 5.6 ≈ 11.1. Below 13 suggests thalassaemia trait rather than iron deficiency; confirm with ferritin and haemoglobin analysis.

cards.f: Which haemoglobin finding confirms β-thalassaemia trait?
cards.b: Raised HbA2 on haemoglobin analysis (HPLC or electrophoresis), with microcytosis and a normal or high red cell count.

cards.f: Which antibodies are tested for in pernicious anaemia?
cards.b: Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies (highly specific) and anti-gastric parietal cell antibodies (sensitive but less specific).

cards.f: Why must B12 be replaced before folate in combined deficiency?
cards.b: Folate alone can correct the anaemia while B12-dependent neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration of the cord) progresses.

cards.f: List four laboratory markers of haemolysis.
cards.b: Raised reticulocytes, raised unconjugated bilirubin, raised LDH and low or absent haptoglobin; also urinary urobilinogen, and haemoglobinuria in intravascular haemolysis.

cards.f: Warm vs cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia?
cards.b: Warm: IgG antibodies active at body temperature, extravascular splenic haemolysis, spherocytes; linked to CLL, SLE, drugs. Cold: IgM fixing complement at low temperatures, agglutination, acrocyanosis; linked to Mycoplasma, EBV and lymphoproliferative disease.

cards.f: Name four oxidant triggers of haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
cards.b: Fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, some sulfonamides and quinolones, and infection; any four.

cards.f: What is the molecular defect in sickle cell disease?
cards.b: A point mutation in β-globin replacing glutamic acid with valine at position 6 (HbS); deoxygenated HbS polymerises, deforming red cells and causing haemolysis and vaso-occlusion.

cards.f: How does hydroxycarbamide help in sickle cell disease?
cards.b: It raises HbF, which does not take part in HbS polymerisation, reducing painful crises and acute chest syndrome; it also lowers neutrophil count and adhesion.

cards.f: What causes an aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease?
cards.b: Parvovirus B19 infects red cell precursors and temporarily stops erythropoiesis; with shortened red cell survival, haemoglobin falls sharply with very low reticulocytes.

cards.f: Describe the genetics of α-thalassaemia syndromes.
cards.b: Four α-globin genes: loss of one is silent, two causes trait (mild microcytosis), three causes HbH disease (β4 tetramers, haemolytic anaemia), four causes Hb Barts hydrops fetalis.

cards.f: Which factors does the PT measure, and which the APTT?
cards.b: PT: VII plus the common pathway (X, V, II, fibrinogen). APTT: XII, XI, IX, VIII plus the common pathway.

cards.f: Which clotting factors are vitamin K dependent?
cards.b: Factors II, VII, IX and X, and the anticoagulant proteins C and S.

cards.f: What does a mixing study show?
cards.b: If a prolonged clotting time corrects when patient plasma is mixed with normal plasma, a factor deficiency is likely; if it does not correct, an inhibitor (e.g. lupus anticoagulant or acquired factor VIII antibody) is present.

cards.f: Contrast the bleeding pattern of platelet disorders and coagulation factor disorders.
cards.b: Platelet and vWF disorders cause immediate mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, epistaxis, menorrhagia). Factor deficiencies cause deep bleeding (haemarthroses, muscle haematomas) and delayed bleeding after injury.

cards.f: Inheritance and deficient factor in haemophilia A and B?
cards.b: Both are X-linked recessive: haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency, haemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.

cards.f: How does emicizumab work?
cards.b: It is a bispecific monoclonal antibody that binds factor IXa and factor X, mimicking the cofactor function of factor VIIIa. It is used as prophylaxis in haemophilia A, including patients with inhibitors.

cards.f: What are the two main functions of von Willebrand factor?
cards.b: It mediates platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen via GPIb, and carries and stabilises factor VIII in plasma.

cards.f: How does desmopressin help some bleeding disorders?
cards.b: It releases stored von Willebrand factor and factor VIII from endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies; useful in type 1 von Willebrand disease and mild haemophilia A.

cards.f: What is the underlying defect in TTP?
cards.b: Severe deficiency of ADAMTS13 (usually an autoantibody), the protease that cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers; ultra-large multimers cause platelet microthrombi.

cards.f: Typical laboratory picture of DIC?
cards.b: Low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, markedly raised D-dimer, and schistocytes on the film.

cards.f: When does HIT typically occur and what is its main danger?
cards.b: Usually 5–10 days after starting heparin (sooner with recent exposure). Antibodies against PF4–heparin complexes activate platelets, so the main danger is thrombosis, not bleeding.

cards.f: Name three inherited thrombophilias.
cards.b: Factor V Leiden (activated protein C resistance), prothrombin G20210A mutation, and deficiencies of antithrombin, protein C or protein S.

cards.f: How does tranexamic acid work?
cards.b: It is an antifibrinolytic that blocks lysine-binding sites on plasminogen, preventing plasmin from binding and degrading fibrin.

cards.f: Why can a patient with lupus anticoagulant have a prolonged APTT yet be at risk of thrombosis?
cards.b: The antibody interferes with phospholipid-dependent clotting tests in vitro, prolonging the APTT, but in vivo antiphospholipid antibodies activate endothelium, platelets and complement, promoting thrombosis.

cards.f: Which translocation defines CML and what does it produce?
cards.b: t(9;22), the Philadelphia chromosome, creating the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase; targeted by imatinib and other TKIs.

cards.f: Why is acute promyelocytic leukaemia an emergency?
cards.b: It commonly causes DIC with life-threatening bleeding. All-trans retinoic acid should be started as soon as it is suspected, with arsenic trioxide, alongside supportive blood products.

cards.f: Name the characteristic cell of Hodgkin lymphoma and its markers.
cards.b: The Reed–Sternberg cell, a large binucleate or multinucleate B-cell-derived cell, typically CD15+ and CD30+.

cards.f: What are B symptoms?
cards.b: Unexplained fevers, drenching night sweats, and weight loss of more than 10% of body weight over 6 months; they indicate a worse prognosis in lymphoma.

cards.f: Match these translocations to lymphomas: t(14;18), t(8;14), t(11;14).
cards.b: t(14;18): follicular lymphoma (BCL2). t(8;14): Burkitt lymphoma (MYC). t(11;14): mantle cell lymphoma (cyclin D1).

cards.f: What does CRAB stand for in myeloma?
cards.b: Hypercalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia and Bone lesions (lytic): the classic myeloma-defining end-organ features.

cards.f: What are the SLiM criteria in myeloma?
cards.b: Biomarkers defining myeloma without CRAB features: at least 60% clonal marrow plasma cells, involved:uninvolved serum free light-chain ratio of 100 or more, or more than one focal lesion on MRI.

cards.f: Typical immunophenotype and film appearance of CLL?
cards.b: Mature B cells co-expressing CD5, CD19 and CD23, with smudge (smear) cells on the blood film.

cards.f: What is Richter transformation?
cards.b: Transformation of CLL into an aggressive lymphoma, usually diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, often presenting with rapid node enlargement, B symptoms and rising LDH.

cards.f: Which mutation is found in almost all cases of polycythaemia vera?
cards.b: JAK2 mutation, usually V617F; most of the remainder have JAK2 exon 12 mutations.

cards.f: List the metabolic features of tumour lysis syndrome.
cards.b: Hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia (secondary to phosphate) and hyperuricaemia, often with AKI.

cards.f: Why is rasburicase avoided in G6PD deficiency?
cards.b: Rasburicase converts urate to allantoin, producing hydrogen peroxide; in G6PD deficiency this oxidant stress causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

cards.f: How should suspected neutropenic sepsis be managed?
cards.b: As a medical emergency: empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin with tazobactam per NICE CG151) immediately, without waiting for the neutrophil count, plus cultures and sepsis assessment.

cards.f: What is MGUS?
cards.b: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance: a small paraprotein with fewer than 10% clonal marrow plasma cells and no myeloma-defining events; it progresses to myeloma or related disorders at about 1% per year.

questions.q: Which cell is primarily responsible for bone resorption?
questions.why: Osteoclasts are multinucleated cells of monocyte–macrophage lineage that resorb bone; osteoblasts form it and osteocytes regulate remodelling.

questions.q: Which Salter–Harris type of physeal fracture is the most common?
questions.why: Type II fractures pass through the physis and exit through the metaphysis (Thurston–Holland fragment) and are the most frequent physeal injuries.

questions.q: Aspiration of an inflamed knee in an 80-year-old woman shows rhomboid crystals that are weakly positively birefringent under polarised light. What is the diagnosis?
questions.why: CPP crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent; urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent.

questions.q: Which examination test is most sensitive for an anterior cruciate ligament tear?
questions.why: Lachman's test assesses anterior tibial translation at about 20–30° of knee flexion; McMurray's tests the menisci, posterior sag the PCL, and patellar tap an effusion.

questions.q: A patient stands on her left leg and the right side of her pelvis drops. Which muscle group is most likely weak?
options: Left hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus)
questions.why: The abductors of the stance leg stabilise the pelvis; if the left abductors are weak, the pelvis drops on the opposite (right) side, a positive Trendelenburg test on the left.

questions.q: Which of the following shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the left?
questions.why: Carbon monoxide increases the oxygen affinity of the remaining haem sites (left shift) as well as reducing carrying capacity; the other options all shift the curve to the right.

questions.q: Which antibody test is most specific for pernicious anaemia?
questions.why: Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific for pernicious anaemia; anti-parietal cell antibodies are more sensitive but occur in other conditions and in some healthy older people.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman of Mediterranean ancestry has Hb 112 g/L, MCV 66 fL, red cell count 6.0 × 10¹²/L and a normal ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Marked microcytosis with a high red cell count and normal ferritin points to thalassaemia trait; the Mentzer index is 66 ÷ 6.0 = 11, below 13. Raised HbA2 would confirm β-thalassaemia trait.

questions.q: Deficiency of which clotting factor prolongs the PT but not the APTT?
questions.why: Factor VII is tested only by the PT; factors VIII and IX are in the APTT pathway, and factor X is in the common pathway, so it prolongs both.

questions.q: The Philadelphia chromosome, t(9;22), is characteristic of which condition?
questions.why: t(9;22) creates the BCR::ABL1 fusion tyrosine kinase that drives CML and is targeted by imatinib; it also occurs in a subset of ALL.

questions.q: Which of the following is a myeloma-defining biomarker (SLiM criterion) in the IMWG 2014 criteria, even without CRAB features?
options: Involved:uninvolved serum free light-chain ratio of 100 or more
Bone marrow clonal plasma cells of 20%
questions.why: The SLiM criteria are at least 60% clonal marrow plasma cells, a free light-chain ratio of 100 or more, or more than one focal MRI lesion. β2-microglobulin is a prognostic marker, not a defining event.

questions.q: Describe and explain the typical serum calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and PTH findings in osteoporosis, osteomalacia, Paget's disease and primary hyperparathyroidism.
markScheme: Osteoporosis: calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH all normal, because mineralisation and mineral homeostasis are intact; the problem is reduced bone mass.
Osteomalacia (vitamin D deficiency): calcium low or low-normal, phosphate low and PTH raised (secondary hyperparathyroidism increases renal phosphate loss); ALP raised from osteoblast activity.
Paget's disease: isolated raised ALP reflecting high bone turnover, with normal calcium and phosphate (calcium may rise with immobilisation).
Primary hyperparathyroidism: high calcium, low or low-normal phosphate, PTH raised or inappropriately normal; ALP normal or raised if bone disease is significant.
questions.modelAnswer: In osteoporosis bone mass is reduced but mineral handling is normal, so calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH are all normal. In osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency, poor gut absorption lowers calcium. Secondary hyperparathyroidism follows, increasing renal phosphate loss so phosphate is low, and active osteoblasts raise ALP. Paget's disease typically shows an isolated rise in ALP from very high bone turnover. Primary hyperparathyroidism produces high calcium with low phosphate and a PTH that is raised or inappropriately normal; ALP rises only with significant bone involvement.

questions.q: Describe the stages of secondary (indirect) fracture healing.
markScheme: Haematoma and inflammation: bleeding forms a haematoma; platelets and inflammatory cells release cytokines and growth factors, recruiting mesenchymal cells (days).
Soft callus: fibroblasts and chondrocytes form granulation tissue and cartilage that bridges the gap and gives some stability (around 2–3 weeks).
Hard callus: endochondral ossification converts cartilage to woven bone, producing clinical and radiological union (weeks to a few months).
Remodelling: osteoclasts and osteoblasts replace woven bone with lamellar bone and restore the medullary canal according to load (Wolff's law), over months to years.
questions.modelAnswer: Secondary healing begins with a haematoma. Platelets and inflammatory cells release cytokines and growth factors that recruit mesenchymal progenitor cells and new blood vessels. Over the next two to three weeks, granulation tissue and cartilage form a soft callus that bridges the fracture and limits movement. The cartilage is then mineralised and replaced by woven bone through endochondral ossification. This forms a hard callus, giving clinical and radiological union. Finally, coupled osteoclast and osteoblast activity remodels the woven bone into lamellar bone, restoring shape and the medullary canal in line with mechanical load.

questions.q: Explain Perren's strain theory and use it to justify different fixation methods for a simple transverse forearm fracture and a comminuted tibial shaft fracture.
markScheme: Strain = change in fracture gap length ÷ original gap length; tissues can only form where strain is below their tolerance.

Very low strain (absolute stability) allows primary bone healing without callus; moderate strain allows callus formation (secondary healing); high strain permits only granulation tissue and leads to non-union.

Simple transverse forearm fracture: a small gap means even slight movement causes high strain, so anatomical reduction with compression plating (absolute stability) is used, healing by primary bone union; forearm rotation also requires precise anatomy.

Comminuted tibial shaft fracture: movement is shared across many fragments and a larger total gap, so strain is lower; relative stability with an intramedullary nail allows callus healing and preserves the soft-tissue and fragment blood supply.
questions.modelAnswer: Perren's theory states that the tissue formed in a fracture gap depends on interfragmentary strain, the change in gap length divided by the original gap. Bone forms only at very low strain, cartilage and fibrous tissue tolerate more, and high strain allows only granulation tissue, leading to non-union. In a simple transverse forearm fracture the gap is tiny, so any movement produces high strain. Anatomical reduction and compression plating give absolute stability and primary healing, and restore the anatomy needed for rotation. In a comminuted tibial fracture, movement is spread across many fragments and a larger total gap, so strain is lower. An intramedullary nail provides relative stability, promotes callus and protects the fragments' blood supply.

questions.q: Compare osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis under four headings: joints affected, stiffness pattern, systemic features and X-ray findings.
markScheme: Joints: OA affects weight-bearing joints, DIP and PIP joints and the first CMC joint, often asymmetrically; RA causes symmetrical small-joint polyarthritis of MCP, PIP, wrist and MTP joints, sparing the DIPs.
Stiffness: OA has pain worse with activity and brief morning stiffness (30 minutes or less); RA has prolonged morning stiffness (over an hour) improving with activity.
Systemic: OA has none; RA may cause fatigue, raised inflammatory markers, rheumatoid nodules, lung and eye disease and raised cardiovascular risk.
X-ray: OA shows joint-space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis and cysts; RA shows periarticular osteopenia, symmetrical joint-space loss and marginal erosions.
questions.modelAnswer: Osteoarthritis affects the knees, hips, DIP and PIP joints and the base of the thumb, often asymmetrically. Rheumatoid arthritis typically causes a symmetrical polyarthritis of the MCP, PIP, wrist and MTP joints and spares the DIPs. OA pain is worse with use and morning stiffness is brief, whereas RA causes prolonged morning stiffness that eases with activity. OA has no systemic features. RA may cause fatigue, raised inflammatory markers, nodules, lung and eye disease and raised cardiovascular risk. On X-ray, OA shows joint-space loss, osteophytes, sclerosis and cysts, while RA shows periarticular osteopenia and marginal erosions.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man has had 4 weeks of swelling of both knees and two MCP joints. Rheumatoid factor is low-positive, anti-CCP negative, and CRP and ESR are normal. Calculate his 2010 ACR/EULAR score and interpret it.
markScheme: Joint involvement: 1–3 small joints (with or without large joints) scores 2.
Serology: low-positive RF scores 2; acute-phase reactants normal score 0; symptom duration under 6 weeks scores 0. Total = 4 out of 10.

Interpretation: below 6, so he does not currently meet classification criteria for RA; criteria are for classification, not diagnosis, so other causes (e.g. reactive, viral, psoriatic arthritis) should be considered and he should be reassessed, as his score may rise with time.
questions.modelAnswer: Joint involvement is scored by the highest category met: any 1–3 small joints, with or without large joints, scores 2. A low-positive rheumatoid factor adds 2. Normal CRP and ESR score 0, and symptoms of under 6 weeks score 0. His total is 4 out of 10. This is below the threshold of 6, so he does not currently meet classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis. The criteria are designed for classification rather than diagnosis, so alternatives such as viral, reactive or psoriatic arthritis should be considered. He should be reassessed, because the duration point alone could change the picture.

questions.q: Outline the components of the GALS screening examination.
markScheme: Three screening questions: pain or stiffness in muscles, joints or back; ability to dress without difficulty; ability to manage stairs without difficulty.
Gait: observe symmetry, smoothness, stride length and ability to turn.
Arms: inspect hands, test grip and pinch, squeeze MCP joints for tenderness, assess shoulder, elbow and wrist movements.
Legs and spine: inspect legs, check knee flexion and effusion, hip internal rotation, squeeze MTP joints; inspect spine curvature, test lumbar flexion and lateral cervical flexion.
questions.modelAnswer: GALS begins with three screening questions: does the patient have pain or stiffness in the muscles, joints or back, and can they dress and manage stairs without difficulty? Gait is observed for symmetry, smoothness and turning. For the arms, inspect the hands, test power and precision grip, squeeze across the MCP joints for tenderness, and assess shoulder, elbow and wrist movement. For the legs, look for deformity and wasting, check knee flexion and effusion and hip internal rotation, and squeeze the MTP joints. Finally, inspect spinal curves from behind and the side and test lumbar flexion and cervical lateral flexion.

questions.q: Explain how erythropoietin production is regulated and why chronic kidney disease causes anaemia.
markScheme: Peritubular interstitial cells of the renal cortex sense oxygen delivery; in hypoxia, hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) escapes degradation by prolyl hydroxylases and increases EPO gene transcription.
EPO acts on erythroid progenitors in the marrow, preventing apoptosis and increasing red cell production, raising oxygen-carrying capacity (negative feedback).
In CKD, loss of functioning renal tissue reduces EPO production relative to the degree of anaemia; uraemia also shortens red cell survival.

Iron deficiency or restriction (raised hepcidin from reduced clearance and inflammation, blood loss) contributes; treatment is iron repletion and erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (or HIF-prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors).
questions.modelAnswer: Peritubular interstitial cells in the renal cortex sense oxygen delivery. In normoxia, prolyl hydroxylases mark hypoxia-inducible factor for destruction. In hypoxia HIF survives and switches on the EPO gene. EPO then stops erythroid progenitors in the marrow from undergoing apoptosis, increasing red cell output until oxygen delivery is restored. In chronic kidney disease, fewer EPO-producing cells mean output is inappropriately low for the degree of anaemia. Uraemia shortens red cell survival, and raised hepcidin from reduced clearance and inflammation restricts iron. Management therefore corrects iron first, then uses erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.

questions.q: Explain the factors that shift the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve, and the physiological or clinical significance of shifts in fetal haemoglobin and carbon monoxide poisoning.
markScheme: The curve is sigmoid because of cooperative binding (T to R state transition); P50 is the PO2 at which haemoglobin is 50% saturated.
Right shift (lower affinity, raised P50): raised PCO2, H⁺ (Bohr effect), temperature and 2,3-BPG; aids unloading in active tissues.
Left shift (higher affinity): the opposite changes, plus HbF and carbon monoxide.
HbF binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so it has higher affinity than maternal HbA, favouring oxygen transfer across the placenta.

Carbon monoxide binds haem with far greater affinity than O2, reducing carrying capacity and left-shifting the curve so the remaining O2 is released less readily; pulse oximetry can be falsely normal, so co-oximetry is needed.
questions.modelAnswer: Haemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively, giving a sigmoid curve described by the P50. Raised PCO2, hydrogen ions, temperature and 2,3-BPG all lower affinity and shift the curve right, which helps oxygen unloading in active tissue. The opposite changes shift it left. Fetal haemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its curve lies left of maternal HbA, and oxygen passes from mother to fetus across the placenta. Carbon monoxide binds haem with far higher affinity than oxygen, cutting carrying capacity and shifting the curve left, so the remaining oxygen is released less readily. Standard pulse oximetry may read normal, so co-oximetry is required.

questions.q: Explain the genetics, mechanism and laboratory diagnosis of G6PD deficiency, including one diagnostic pitfall.
markScheme: X-linked inheritance: mostly affects males; common in people of African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Asian ancestry (protective against malaria).

G6PD generates NADPH in the pentose phosphate pathway, which keeps glutathione reduced; without it, oxidant stress (fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, infection) denatures haemoglobin and damages the membrane, causing acute intravascular haemolysis.
Film shows Heinz bodies (supravital stain) and bite or blister cells; haemolysis markers are raised.
Diagnosis is by G6PD enzyme assay; pitfall: levels may be falsely normal during or soon after haemolysis because reticulocytes have high G6PD activity, so retest a few months later.
questions.modelAnswer: G6PD deficiency is X-linked, so it mainly affects males, and is common where malaria is or was endemic. G6PD produces NADPH, which keeps glutathione reduced and protects red cells from oxidants. Triggers such as fava beans, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase or infection then oxidise haemoglobin, which precipitates as Heinz bodies, and the membrane is damaged, causing acute haemolysis. The blood film shows bite and blister cells, and haemolysis markers rise. Diagnosis rests on an enzyme assay. During an acute episode, the surviving young cells and reticulocytes have high enzyme activity, so the result may be falsely normal and should be repeated after recovery.

questions.q: Describe the steps of primary and secondary haemostasis.
markScheme: Primary: vasoconstriction and platelet adhesion to exposed subendothelial collagen via vWF binding glycoprotein Ib.
Platelet activation releases ADP and thromboxane A2, recruiting more platelets; aggregation via GPIIb/IIIa binding fibrinogen forms the platelet plug.
Secondary: tissue factor exposed at the injury binds factor VIIa, generating initial thrombin; thrombin amplifies the response by activating platelets and factors V, VIII and XI.
Tenase (IXa–VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa–Va) on the platelet surface produce a thrombin burst; fibrinogen is converted to fibrin and cross-linked by factor XIIIa, stabilising the clot.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary haemostasis forms the platelet plug. After vasoconstriction, platelets adhere to exposed collagen through von Willebrand factor binding glycoprotein Ib. They then activate and release ADP and thromboxane A2, recruiting further platelets that aggregate as GPIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen. Secondary haemostasis builds the fibrin mesh. Tissue factor exposed at the wound binds factor VIIa and generates a little thrombin. That thrombin activates platelets and factors V, VIII and XI. On the platelet surface, the tenase and prothrombinase complexes then generate a burst of thrombin, converting fibrinogen to fibrin, which factor XIIIa cross-links.

questions.q: Explain the pathophysiology, laboratory features and prevention of tumour lysis syndrome.
markScheme: Rapid breakdown of tumour cells, usually after starting treatment for high-grade, bulky or high-count malignancies (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL, AML with high white count), releases intracellular contents.
Laboratory features: hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, secondary hypocalcaemia (calcium phosphate precipitation) and hyperuricaemia (nucleic acid breakdown via xanthine oxidase).
AKI results from uric acid and calcium phosphate crystal deposition in tubules; arrhythmia and seizures are the main life-threatening risks.

Prevention: risk assessment, vigorous IV hydration, allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) for intermediate risk or rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) for high risk, avoiding rasburicase in G6PD deficiency; frequent electrolyte monitoring.
questions.modelAnswer: Tumour lysis syndrome occurs when large numbers of malignant cells break down quickly, usually soon after treatment of bulky or rapidly proliferating cancers such as Burkitt lymphoma or acute leukaemia with a high white count. The released potassium and phosphate cause hyperkalaemia and hyperphosphataemia. Phosphate binds calcium, causing hypocalcaemia, and nucleic acids are metabolised to uric acid. Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals deposit in the renal tubules, causing AKI, and arrhythmias or seizures can follow. Prevention involves identifying high-risk patients, vigorous IV hydration, and allopurinol or, for high risk, rasburicase (not in G6PD deficiency), with frequent electrolyte checks.

questions.q:
Mrs Walsh, a 68-year-old woman, falls from standing and sustains a distal radius fracture. She has taken oral prednisolone for polymyalgia rheumatica for 18 months. She smokes and her mother had a hip fracture. DXA shows a femoral neck T-score of −2.8 and lumbar spine T-score of −3.1. Serum calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH are normal; 25-hydroxyvitamin D is mildly low.

(a) Define osteoporosis and interpret her results. (b) Explain how glucocorticoids cause bone loss. (c) Outline her management, including the mechanism, administration counselling and important adverse effects of first-line drug therapy. (d) Describe two alternative drug options and a key safety consideration for each.
markScheme: WHO definition: BMD T-score of −2.5 or lower (SD below young adult mean) at hip or spine; with a fragility fracture this is established (severe) osteoporosis.

Normal bone biochemistry argues against osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism or Paget's; mildly low vitamin D needs correction; consider secondary causes (e.g. myeloma screen, thyroid, coeliac, testosterone/oestrogen status as appropriate).

Risk factors: glucocorticoids, smoking, parental hip fracture, prior fragility fracture; FRAX and NOGG (2022) thresholds guide treatment; fragility fracture plus glucocorticoid use places her at high risk.

Glucocorticoids suppress osteoblast formation and function and promote osteoblast/osteocyte apoptosis (main effect); increase RANKL and reduce OPG, enhancing resorption; reduce gut calcium absorption and sex hormone levels; cause myopathy and falls.
Fracture risk rises early in therapy and partly independent of BMD; review the glucocorticoid and use the lowest effective exposure or steroid-sparing therapy.
Lifestyle: stop smoking, limit alcohol, weight-bearing and balance exercise, falls assessment; ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D.

First-line oral bisphosphonate (e.g. alendronate): binds hydroxyapatite and is taken up by osteoclasts; nitrogen-containing agents inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, causing osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis.
Counselling: take on an empty stomach with plain water, remain upright and delay food or other medicines as directed, to reduce oesophageal injury and ensure absorption.

Adverse effects: oesophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw (dental review), atypical femoral fractures (report thigh or groin pain); avoid in severe renal impairment; reassess need after a period of treatment (drug holiday review).

Alternatives: denosumab (RANKL antibody) — hypocalcaemia, ONJ, and rebound vertebral fractures if stopped without follow-on therapy; teriparatide (anabolic PTH analogue) for very high or glucocorticoid-associated risk — intermittent exposure stimulates osteoblasts; romosozumab (sclerostin antibody) — avoid after MI or stroke.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The WHO defines osteoporosis as a bone mineral density T-score of −2.5 or lower at the hip or spine. Mrs Walsh's scores of −2.8 and −3.1, together with a fragility fracture, indicate established osteoporosis. Normal calcium, phosphate, ALP and PTH make osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism and Paget's disease unlikely. Her mildly low vitamin D needs correction, and secondary causes such as myeloma, thyroid disease and coeliac disease should be considered. Glucocorticoids, smoking, a parental hip fracture and her own fracture place her at high risk on FRAX and NOGG thresholds.

(b) Glucocorticoids mainly suppress bone formation by inhibiting osteoblast recruitment and function and promoting osteoblast and osteocyte apoptosis. They also raise RANKL and lower OPG, increasing resorption. Gut calcium absorption falls, sex hormones fall, and steroid myopathy raises falls risk. Fracture risk rises within months of starting and is greater than BMD predicts.

(c) The need for prednisolone and the lowest effective exposure should be reviewed with her rheumatologist. She should stop smoking, do weight-bearing and balance exercise, have a falls assessment and take adequate calcium and vitamin D. First-line therapy is an oral bisphosphonate such as alendronate. It binds hydroxyapatite and is taken up by osteoclasts, where it inhibits farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase, causing osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis. She should take it on an empty stomach with plain water, remain upright and delay food and other medicines, to protect the oesophagus and allow absorption. Adverse effects include oesophagitis, osteonecrosis of the jaw (a dental check is advisable) and atypical femoral fractures, so she should report new thigh or groin pain. Treatment should be reviewed after several years.

(d) Denosumab, a RANKL antibody, is an alternative, but stopping it without follow-on bisphosphonate causes rebound vertebral fractures. Hypocalcaemia must also be corrected first. Teriparatide is an anabolic PTH analogue whose intermittent action stimulates osteoblasts. It is well suited to very high risk or glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, but treatment is time-limited and should be followed by an antiresorptive.

questions.q:
Callum, a 24-year-old motorcyclist, is brought in after a collision. His right lower leg is deformed, with a 3 cm wound over the mid-shin through which bone is visible; there is little visible contamination. Foot pulses are present and sensation is intact. X-ray shows a displaced transverse fracture of the tibial shaft. After initial management he is admitted. Twelve hours later he reports severe pain despite morphine and cannot tolerate passive flexion of his toes. His blood pressure is 120/65 mmHg; anterior compartment pressure is 40 mmHg. Foot pulses remain palpable.

(a) Classify the fracture and describe his immediate management in the emergency department. (b) What complication has developed? Interpret the pressure measurement and explain why palpable pulses do not exclude it. (c) Outline the definitive management of this complication and the consequences of delay.
markScheme: Open fracture of the tibial shaft; provisional Gustilo–Anderson type II (wound 1–10 cm, moderate soft-tissue injury), with final grading at debridement (high-energy mechanism may upgrade to type III).
ATLS primary survey; analgesia; neurovascular assessment documented before and after any manipulation.
IV antibiotics as soon as possible, ideally within an hour of injury; tetanus prophylaxis as indicated.
Photograph wound, remove gross contamination, cover with saline-soaked dressing; realign and splint the limb; no wound exploration in ED.
Early debridement and stabilisation by combined orthopaedic and plastic surgical team (BOAST/NICE NG37), with plan for soft-tissue cover.

Acute compartment syndrome: rising pressure in a closed fascial compartment impairs venous outflow and capillary perfusion, causing muscle and nerve ischaemia; open fractures do not decompress compartments reliably.
Delta pressure = diastolic − compartment pressure = 65 − 40 = 25 mmHg; below 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis.
Pulses persist because arterial pressure greatly exceeds compartment pressure; tissue ischaemia occurs at capillary level; pulselessness is a late sign.

Management: remove circumferential dressings or casts, keep limb at heart level (not elevated), maintain BP, urgent four-compartment fasciotomy (typically two incisions), wounds left open with delayed closure or grafting.
Delay causes irreversible muscle necrosis and nerve damage within hours, leading to contracture (Volkmann's), rhabdomyolysis with AKI and hyperkalaemia, infection, and amputation.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) This is an open fracture of the tibial shaft. With a 3 cm wound and moderate soft-tissue injury, it is provisionally Gustilo–Anderson type II. Final grading happens at debridement, and the high-energy mechanism may upgrade it to type III. Management begins with an ATLS primary survey. He needs analgesia and a documented neurovascular examination before and after any manipulation. Intravenous antibiotics should be given as soon as possible, ideally within an hour of injury, with tetanus prophylaxis if needed. The wound is photographed, gross contamination removed and a saline-soaked dressing applied. It is not explored in the department. The limb is realigned and splinted. Debridement and skeletal stabilisation should be done early by a combined orthopaedic and plastic surgical team, with a plan for soft-tissue cover.

(b) He has acute compartment syndrome of the leg. Swelling and bleeding within a closed fascial compartment raise pressure until venous outflow and capillary perfusion fail, making muscle and nerve ischaemic. An open wound does not reliably decompress the compartments. Delta pressure is diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure: 65 − 40 = 25 mmHg. Below 30 mmHg supports the diagnosis, and his pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are classic signs. Pulses remain because arterial pressure far exceeds compartment pressure. The ischaemia occurs at capillary level, and loss of pulses is a late sign.

(c) Remove any circumferential dressings or splint padding down to the skin and keep the limb at heart level rather than elevated.
