Maintain blood pressure, and arrange urgent fasciotomy decompressing all four compartments, usually through two incisions. The wounds are left open and closed or grafted later. Delay causes irreversible muscle necrosis and nerve injury within hours. Rhabdomyolysis can then cause hyperkalaemia and AKI, and later problems include contracture, infection, chronic disability and amputation.

questions.q:
Mrs Bennett, an 84-year-old woman, is found on the floor at home. Her left leg is shortened and externally rotated. She lives alone, walks outdoors independently with one stick and has no cognitive impairment; she has hypertension controlled with amlodipine. X-ray shows a displaced intracapsular fracture of the left femoral neck (Garden IV).

(a) Explain why the type of hip fracture determines whether it is fixed or replaced, with reference to the blood supply of the femoral head. (b) Describe her perioperative management according to NICE CG124. (c) What operation is appropriate for her, and why? (d) Outline secondary prevention and rehabilitation.
markScheme: Femoral head blood supply mainly from retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running along the femoral neck within the capsule; artery of ligamentum teres contributes little in adults.
Displaced intracapsular fractures disrupt retinacular vessels, giving high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union, so the head is replaced (arthroplasty).

Undisplaced intracapsular fractures may be fixed (screws), and extracapsular fractures (blood supply preserved) are fixed with a sliding hip screw (trochanteric) or intramedullary nail (subtrochanteric).
Garden classification: I–II undisplaced, III–IV displaced.

Perioperative: prompt analgesia (paracetamol, opioids as needed, regional nerve block such as fascia iliaca), fluids, assessment of cause of fall (syncope, arrhythmia), check for long-lie complications (rhabdomyolysis, pressure areas, hypothermia).
Surgery on the day of or day after admission; correct correctable comorbidities without unnecessary delay; orthogeriatric involvement from admission.
VTE prophylaxis, delirium prevention and screening, nutrition, pressure-area care.

Total hip replacement rather than hemiarthroplasty, because she can walk independently outdoors with no more than a stick, is not cognitively impaired and is medically fit (CG124 criteria); offers better function.
Mobilisation the day after surgery, multidisciplinary rehabilitation, discharge planning.

Secondary prevention: falls risk assessment and intervention; bone health assessment and osteoporosis treatment (hip fragility fracture usually justifies treatment without waiting for DXA); vitamin D and calcium.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) In adults the femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery. These run up the femoral neck within the joint capsule, and the artery of the ligamentum teres contributes little. A displaced intracapsular fracture tears these vessels, so the head is at high risk of avascular necrosis and non-union, and is replaced rather than fixed. Undisplaced intracapsular fractures (Garden I–II) can sometimes be fixed. Extracapsular fractures leave the blood supply intact and are fixed: trochanteric fractures with a sliding hip screw, subtrochanteric fractures with an intramedullary nail.

(b) She needs prompt analgesia with paracetamol and opioids as required, plus a regional block such as a fascia iliaca block, which reduces opioid needs. Look for the cause of the fall, such as syncope or arrhythmia, and for long-lie complications: rhabdomyolysis, pressure damage, dehydration and hypothermia. NICE CG124 recommends surgery on the day of, or day after, admission. Correctable problems should be treated without unnecessary delay. An orthogeriatrician should be involved from admission. Care should include VTE prophylaxis, delirium prevention and screening, nutrition and pressure-area care.

(c) A total hip replacement is appropriate. NICE recommends it over hemiarthroplasty for displaced intracapsular fractures in patients who walk independently outdoors with no more than a stick, are not cognitively impaired and are medically fit for the procedure. She meets all three criteria, and total hip replacement gives better function and fewer reoperations in such patients.

(d) She should mobilise the day after surgery with physiotherapy. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation and discharge planning, including home assessment, help her return to independence. Secondary prevention includes a multifactorial falls assessment covering medicines, vision, home hazards, and strength and balance. Bone health must be addressed: a hip fragility fracture in a woman of her age usually justifies osteoporosis treatment without waiting for DXA, alongside vitamin D and calcium repletion.

questions.q:
Mr Fletcher, a 67-year-old man with hypertension and stage 3b CKD, takes bendroflumethiazide and ramipril. He presents with a 24-hour history of a hot, swollen, exquisitely painful right knee. He had two previous attacks of big-toe pain. Temperature is 38.2 °C and CRP is raised. Knee aspiration yields turbid fluid; polarised microscopy shows needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals, and the Gram stain shows no organisms. Culture is pending.

(a) What is the most likely diagnosis, and why should septic arthritis still be considered? (b) Explain the pathophysiology of the acute attack. (c) Outline treatment of the flare, taking his comorbidities into account. (d) Describe his long-term management.
markScheme: Most likely acute gout (monosodium urate crystals, negatively birefringent, needle-shaped).

Crystals do not exclude infection: septic and crystal arthritis can coexist; Gram stain is often negative in septic arthritis; fever and raised CRP occur in both; await culture and treat empirically if clinical suspicion is high.

Pathophysiology: urate supersaturation (here worsened by thiazide and CKD reducing excretion) leads to crystal deposition; crystals are phagocytosed and activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, releasing IL-1β and recruiting neutrophils.
Serum urate may be normal during a flare; recheck once settled.

Flare treatment: NSAIDs best avoided given CKD and ACE inhibitor; colchicine with caution and renal adjustment (interactions, e.g. strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors); corticosteroid (oral or intra-articular once infection excluded) is often preferred.
Rest, ice, elevation; continue ULT if already taking it.
Long-term: offer ULT with treat-to-target (NICE NG219): allopurinol first line (or febuxostat), started low and titrated with renal function, target urate below 360 µmol/L.
Colchicine (or alternative) prophylaxis while starting ULT; start ULT once flare settles (or during frequent flares).

Review thiazide: consider an alternative antihypertensive (e.g. losartan has a modest uricosuric effect); lifestyle advice (alcohol, weight, sugary drinks); screen for cardiovascular risk and diabetes.
Patient education on flare management and adherence.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals confirm monosodium urate, so acute gout is the most likely diagnosis. Septic arthritis must still be considered, because crystals and infection can coexist. The Gram stain is often negative in septic arthritis, and fever and raised CRP occur in both conditions. Culture results must be followed up, and if clinical suspicion is high, empirical antibiotics should be started while they are awaited.

(b) Gout follows urate supersaturation. In his case, both the thiazide and CKD reduce renal urate excretion. Monosodium urate crystals deposit in and around joints. When crystals are shed, macrophages phagocytose them, activating the NLRP3 inflammasome and releasing IL-1β. Neutrophils are recruited, causing intense inflammation. Serum urate may fall during a flare, so a normal level does not exclude gout.

(c) NSAIDs are best avoided because of his CKD and ACE inhibitor, which together risk AKI. Colchicine can be used with renal adjustment and attention to interacting drugs. A corticosteroid is often the safest option, given orally or intra-articularly once infection has been excluded. Rest, ice and elevation help.

(d) NICE NG219 recommends offering urate-lowering therapy with a treat-to-target strategy, particularly with CKD, diuretic use and recurrent flares. Allopurinol is first line. It is started low and titrated according to renal function, aiming for serum urate below 360 µmol/L, with febuxostat as an alternative. Colchicine prophylaxis is given while ULT is introduced. ULT is usually started once the flare settles, but can be started during frequent flares. The thiazide should be reviewed: losartan, with a modest uricosuric effect, is one alternative antihypertensive. He needs lifestyle advice on alcohol, sugary drinks and weight, cardiovascular risk assessment, and education about adherence and what to do in a flare.

questions.q: "There is a window of opportunity in rheumatoid arthritis: treat early and intensively, and the course of the disease is fundamentally changed." Critically evaluate this statement.
markScheme: Pathogenesis: genetic risk (HLA-DRB1 shared epitope) and environmental triggers (smoking) promote citrullination and ACPA formation, often years before clinical arthritis (pre-clinical phase).
Synovitis with pannus and osteoclast activation causes erosions early; damage is largely irreversible, supporting early intervention.

Evidence for treating early: delays to DMARD therapy associated with worse radiographic and functional outcomes; NICE NG100 recommends starting conventional DMARDs ideally within 3 months of persistent symptoms.

Evidence for intensive strategies: TICORA (2004) showed tight control improved disease activity and outcomes; BeSt (2005) showed initial combination therapy gave faster response; treat-to-target now standard.
Biologics and JAK inhibitors improve outcomes in active disease but are not usually first line, partly for cost and safety (MHRA 2023 JAK warnings).

Limits: many patients respond well to methotrexate alone, so intensive therapy risks overtreatment and toxicity; sustained drug-free remission remains uncommon, so 'fundamentally changed' is debatable.

Prevention trials in at-risk individuals: abatacept (APIPPRA, 2024) delayed progression while on treatment but benefit waned after stopping; methotrexate in MRI-detected subclinical inflammation (TREAT EARLIER, 2022) improved symptoms but did not prevent arthritis.
Heterogeneity: seropositive and seronegative RA differ; definitions of 'early' vary; observational data are confounded.
Benefits beyond joints: controlling inflammation may reduce cardiovascular risk.
Balanced conclusion: early treat-to-target clearly improves outcomes, but evidence that a time-limited window permanently alters disease biology is incomplete.
questions.modelAnswer:
Rheumatoid arthritis begins long before swollen joints appear. People with HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles who are exposed to triggers such as smoking may develop citrullinated proteins and anti-CCP antibodies years earlier. Once synovitis is established, pannus and osteoclast activation erode cartilage and bone within months, and that damage is largely irreversible. Such a time course suggests early treatment matters.

The evidence supports early and intensive treatment improving outcomes. Delays in starting DMARDs are associated with more radiographic damage and disability. NICE NG100 therefore recommends a conventional DMARD, ideally within three months of persistent symptoms. TICORA (2004) showed that intensive, target-driven management achieved lower disease activity and better outcomes than routine care. BeSt (2005) found that initial combination therapy produced faster improvement in function and less early radiographic progression, although later outcomes converged across strategies. Treat-to-target, with regular measurement and escalation, is now standard.

The statement nonetheless overreaches. 'Fundamentally changed' implies an altered disease course, yet sustained drug-free remission remains uncommon, and most patients need lifelong therapy. Intensive regimens risk overtreating patients who would respond to methotrexate alone, with added toxicity. Biologics and JAK inhibitors are costly, and the MHRA (2023) restricted JAK inhibitors in higher-risk groups. Trials in at-risk individuals are telling. In APIPPRA (2024), abatacept delayed the onset of arthritis while it was given, but the effect waned afterwards. In TREAT EARLIER (2022), methotrexate in people with MRI-detected subclinical inflammation improved symptoms and function but did not prevent clinical arthritis. These results suggest treatment suppresses disease rather than resetting it. 'Early' is also defined inconsistently, and seropositive and seronegative disease behave differently.

In conclusion, early treat-to-target therapy clearly reduces damage and disability and may lower cardiovascular risk. The stronger claim, that a fixed window exists in which treatment permanently changes disease biology, is not yet proven. The practical lesson is rapid referral, early DMARDs and tight control tailored to the individual.

questions.q:
Mr Hughes, a 42-year-old warehouse worker, has had low back pain for a week after lifting. Over 24 hours he has developed pain radiating down both legs, numbness "around his bottom" and difficulty passing urine. On examination there is reduced pinprick sensation in the perianal and buttock region, weakness of ankle plantarflexion bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes and reduced anal tone. Straight leg raise is positive at 40° on both sides. A bladder scan after voiding shows a large residual volume.

(a) Interpret the neurological findings, identifying the likely roots involved. (b) What is the diagnosis and the probable underlying cause? (c) Outline immediate management. (d) List other red flags in back pain and the conditions they suggest.
markScheme: Saddle (perianal) sensory loss indicates S2–S4 involvement; reduced anal tone and urinary retention reflect sacral parasympathetic and somatic dysfunction.
Weak plantarflexion and absent ankle reflexes indicate S1 root involvement bilaterally.
Positive bilateral straight leg raise indicates nerve root tension of the lower lumbar/sacral roots (L5–S1).
Diagnosis: cauda equina syndrome with retention (CES-R), most likely from a large central lumbar disc prolapse (commonly L4/5 or L5/S1).
Emergency MRI of the lumbar spine without delay (regardless of time of day).
Urgent referral to spinal surgery for decompression (discectomy); earlier decompression is associated with better bladder outcomes, especially before retention is established.
Catheterise and document residual volume; document neurological findings, including perianal sensation and anal tone, carefully; analgesia.

Red flags: history of cancer, weight loss, night pain (malignancy); fever, IV drug use, immunosuppression (infection, e.g. discitis, epidural abscess); trauma, osteoporosis, steroid use (fracture); young age, morning stiffness, improvement with exercise (inflammatory spondyloarthritis); progressive neurological deficit.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Reduced perianal and buttock sensation is saddle anaesthesia, reflecting S2–S4 dysfunction. Reduced anal tone and urinary retention also point to the sacral roots supplying the bladder and sphincters. Bilateral weak plantarflexion and absent ankle reflexes show S1 involvement on both sides. A bilateral positive straight leg raise indicates tension on the lower lumbar and sacral roots. Findings on both sides across several sacral roots localise the lesion to the cauda equina rather than to a single root.

(b) This is cauda equina syndrome with established urinary retention, sometimes called CES-R. In a man of 42 with symptoms after lifting, the likely cause is a large central lumbar disc prolapse, most often at L4/5 or L5/S1, compressing several roots of the cauda equina.

(c) This is a surgical emergency. He needs an MRI of the lumbar spine as an emergency, whatever the time of day, and immediate referral to the on-call spinal surgical team for decompression, usually discectomy. Outcomes for bladder, bowel and sexual function are better with earlier decompression, especially before retention is established. Meanwhile he should be catheterised and the residual volume recorded. Neurological findings, including perianal sensation and anal tone, should be carefully documented for later comparison, and adequate analgesia given.

(d) Other red flags include a history of cancer, unexplained weight loss or night pain, suggesting malignancy. Fever, intravenous drug use or immunosuppression suggests discitis or an epidural abscess. Significant trauma, osteoporosis or long-term steroid use suggests vertebral fracture. Young onset, prolonged morning stiffness and improvement with exercise suggest inflammatory spondyloarthritis. Progressive neurological deficit also needs urgent assessment.

questions.q: "Hepcidin is the master regulator of iron, and most disorders of iron balance are really disorders of hepcidin." Discuss.
markScheme: Hepcidin is a liver-derived peptide that binds ferroportin, causing its internalisation and degradation; this reduces iron export from enterocytes, macrophages and hepatocytes.
Regulation upwards: iron loading via BMP6, haemojuvelin, HFE and transferrin receptor 2 signalling through SMAD; inflammation via IL-6 and STAT3.
Regulation downwards: increased erythropoietic demand (erythroferrone from erythroblasts), hypoxia, and iron deficiency (matriptase-2/TMPRSS6 activity).
HFE haemochromatosis (and other hereditary haemochromatosis types): inappropriately low hepcidin causes excessive absorption and parenchymal iron overload.
Anaemia of inflammation: IL-6-driven hepcidin traps iron in macrophages and reduces absorption, giving low serum iron with normal or high ferritin.
β-thalassaemia (including non-transfusion-dependent): ineffective erythropoiesis raises erythroferrone, suppressing hepcidin and causing iron overload even without transfusion.
IRIDA: TMPRSS6 mutations cause inappropriately high hepcidin and iron deficiency refractory to oral iron; CKD anaemia partly reflects raised hepcidin.

Counterpoints: the commonest iron disorder, iron deficiency from blood loss or poor intake, is not primarily a hepcidin disorder (hepcidin responds appropriately); transfusional iron overload and ferroportin disease bypass or involve the target rather than hepcidin.

Clinical implications: oral iron transiently raises hepcidin, so less frequent (e.g. alternate-day) dosing may improve absorption; IV iron bypasses the gut block; hepcidin-targeted therapies are in development.
Balanced conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Hepcidin is a small peptide made by the liver. It binds ferroportin, the only known cellular iron exporter, causing it to be internalised and degraded. When hepcidin is high, enterocytes absorb less iron and macrophages and hepatocytes retain it. When hepcidin is low, iron floods into plasma. Hepcidin integrates several signals. Iron loading raises it through BMP6 and haemojuvelin signalling via SMAD proteins, supported by HFE and transferrin receptor 2. Inflammation raises it through IL-6 and STAT3. Erythropoietic demand suppresses it through erythroferrone released by erythroblasts, and hypoxia and iron deficiency suppress it via matriptase-2 (TMPRSS6).

Many conditions are well explained by abnormal hepcidin. In HFE haemochromatosis, hepcidin is inappropriately low for body iron, so absorption continues and iron accumulates in the liver, heart and pancreas. In anaemia of inflammation, IL-6-driven hepcidin traps iron in macrophages and blocks absorption, giving low serum iron with normal or high ferritin. In β-thalassaemia, ineffective erythropoiesis produces excess erythroferrone, suppressing hepcidin and causing iron overload even in patients who are rarely transfused. Iron-refractory iron deficiency anaemia (IRIDA), from TMPRSS6 mutations, shows the reverse: inappropriately high hepcidin and iron deficiency unresponsive to oral iron. Raised hepcidin also contributes to the anaemia of CKD.

The statement overreaches, however. The commonest iron disorder worldwide is iron deficiency from blood loss, pregnancy or poor intake. Hepcidin falls appropriately in that case, and the problem is supply, not regulation. Transfusional iron overload bypasses absorption entirely, and ferroportin disease involves the target of hepcidin rather than the hormone itself.

The hepcidin model still has practical value. Oral iron transiently raises hepcidin, which is why less frequent, for example alternate-day, dosing may improve fractional absorption. Intravenous iron bypasses the gut block in inflammation and IRIDA, and therapies that mimic or inhibit hepcidin are being developed.

In conclusion, hepcidin is the central regulator of systemic iron and explains many disorders of distribution and overload. Yet 'most disorders' is too strong when simple iron loss remains the dominant clinical problem.

questions.q:
Mrs Lyons, a 66-year-old woman with hypothyroidism and vitiligo, has 4 months of tiredness, a sore tongue, tingling in both feet and unsteadiness that is worse in the dark. Romberg's test is positive and vibration sense is reduced to the knees. FBC: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 118 fL, WCC and platelets mildly low. The film shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Serum B12 is low, folate normal, LDH raised and bilirubin mildly raised.

(a) What is the most likely diagnosis and cause? (b) Explain the haematological and neurological effects of B12 deficiency, including the raised LDH and bilirubin. (c) Which investigations would confirm the cause? (d) Outline management and follow-up.
markScheme: Diagnosis: megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency, most likely pernicious anaemia (autoimmune; associated hypothyroidism and vitiligo).

B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase; deficiency traps folate as methyl-tetrahydrofolate (folate trap), impairing thymidine and DNA synthesis while RNA synthesis continues, giving nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony and macrocytosis.
Pancytopenia and hypersegmented neutrophils reflect impaired DNA synthesis in all lineages.
Ineffective erythropoiesis (intramedullary destruction of abnormal precursors) raises LDH and unconjugated bilirubin.

Neurology: B12 is also a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; deficiency impairs myelin, causing subacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns: loss of vibration and proprioception, positive Romberg; corticospinal tracts) and peripheral neuropathy; cognitive change possible.

Confirm cause: anti-intrinsic factor antibodies first (specific; a negative result does not exclude autoimmune gastritis), with anti-parietal cell antibodies (sensitive, less specific) if suspicion remains, as in NICE NG239; raised methylmalonic acid or homocysteine if B12 result equivocal; consider other causes (diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease, metformin).

Management: parenteral (IM) hydroxocobalamin with initial loading then lifelong maintenance, given more intensively while neurological deficit is improving; oral therapy is unsuitable as initial treatment for pernicious anaemia with neurology.
Do not give folate alone before B12 (risk of worsening neurology); monitor potassium early in treatment (hypokalaemia as new cells take up K⁺); reticulocyte response within about a week.
Follow-up: FBC recovery, neurological review; screen for associated autoimmune disease; increased gastric cancer and neuroendocrine tumour risk (low threshold for endoscopy with symptoms).
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Macrocytic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, mild pancytopenia and a low B12 indicates megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 deficiency. With hypothyroidism and vitiligo, the likely cause is pernicious anaemia, an autoimmune gastritis that destroys parietal cells and intrinsic factor.

(b) B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase, which regenerates tetrahydrofolate from methyl-tetrahydrofolate. Without it, folate is trapped in the methyl form, thymidine synthesis falls and DNA replication slows while RNA and cytoplasmic growth continue. The result is large cells with immature nuclei in every lineage: macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils and low counts. Many abnormal precursors are destroyed in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis), releasing LDH and producing unconjugated bilirubin. B12 is also a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and its deficiency impairs myelin. This causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord, with dorsal column loss of vibration and proprioception, a positive Romberg test and corticospinal signs, plus peripheral neuropathy and sometimes cognitive change.

(c) Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific for pernicious anaemia. A negative result does not exclude the diagnosis; anti-parietal cell antibodies are more sensitive but less specific, and NICE NG239 reserves them for when suspicion remains after a negative intrinsic factor antibody test. If the B12 result is borderline, raised methylmalonic acid or homocysteine supports deficiency. Dietary history, previous gastric or ileal surgery and medicines such as metformin should be reviewed.

(d) Because she has neurological involvement, treatment is intramuscular hydroxocobalamin. It is given intensively at first, continued while neurology improves, then maintained for life. Folate must not be given alone before B12 is replaced. Potassium should be checked early, because rapid new red cell production can cause hypokalaemia. A reticulocyte response is expected within about a week, with recovery of the blood count over weeks. Neurological recovery is slower and may be incomplete. She should be monitored for other autoimmune disease. Because pernicious anaemia increases the risk of gastric cancer, new upper GI symptoms warrant a low threshold for endoscopy.

questions.q:
Kwame, a 19-year-old man with sickle cell anaemia (HbSS), presents with 2 days of bone pain followed by pleuritic chest pain, cough and fever of 38.6 °C. His respiratory rate is 30/min and SpO2 89% on air. Chest X-ray shows new bilateral lower-zone consolidation. Hb is 62 g/L (usual 85 g/L), reticulocytes are raised and WCC is elevated.

(a) What is the diagnosis? Explain the molecular basis of sickling and the pathophysiology of this complication. (b) Outline his acute management. (c) Explain the role of transfusion, distinguishing simple and exchange transfusion. (d) Describe long-term measures to reduce complications in sickle cell disease.
markScheme: Diagnosis: acute chest syndrome (new pulmonary infiltrate with fever and/or respiratory symptoms in a patient with sickle cell disease).

Molecular basis: β-globin Glu6Val mutation produces HbS, which polymerises when deoxygenated, making red cells rigid and sickle-shaped; sickling is promoted by hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration and cold.

Pathophysiology: vicious cycle of infection (including atypical organisms), fat embolism from infarcted bone marrow, and hypoventilation from rib infarction or opioid sedation causing hypoxia, which promotes further sickling and pulmonary vaso-occlusion; adhesion of sickle cells, leucocytes and endothelium.
Acute: oxygen to maintain saturations, prompt effective analgesia (opioids with monitoring, avoiding oversedation), incentive spirometry, cautious IV fluids avoiding overload.
Antibiotics covering typical and atypical organisms (e.g. a cephalosporin with a macrolide per local policy); blood cultures; VTE prophylaxis.
Early involvement of haematology and critical care; may need ventilatory support.
Simple transfusion raises Hb and oxygen-carrying capacity when Hb has fallen and disease is moderate; avoid raising Hb too high (hyperviscosity).
Exchange transfusion lowers the HbS percentage without raising viscosity; indicated for severe or deteriorating ACS, stroke and multiorgan failure.

Long-term: hydroxycarbamide (raises HbF, reduces crises and ACS), vaccinations and penicillin prophylaxis (functional hyposplenism), folic acid as per local practice, transcranial Doppler screening in children.

Regular transfusion programmes for stroke prevention with iron chelation; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene-editing therapy (exa-cel, authorised by the MHRA in 2023) for selected patients; psychological support and education on triggers.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) New consolidation with fever, chest pain and hypoxia in a patient with sickle cell disease is acute chest syndrome. HbS results from a point mutation substituting valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of β-globin. When deoxygenated, HbS polymerises into long fibres that make red cells rigid and sickle-shaped. Hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration and cold all promote sickling. In acute chest syndrome, infection (including atypical organisms), fat embolism from infarcted marrow, and hypoventilation from rib infarction or opioid sedation all reduce oxygenation. Hypoxia causes more sickling and pulmonary vaso-occlusion, setting up a vicious cycle, and adhesion between sickle cells, leucocytes and endothelium amplifies it.

(b) Give oxygen to maintain target saturations. Provide prompt, effective analgesia with opioids, monitoring sedation and breathing. Use incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis and cautious IV fluids, avoiding overload. Start antibiotics covering typical and atypical organisms, such as a cephalosporin with a macrolide according to local policy, after blood cultures. He also needs VTE prophylaxis. Haematology and critical care should be involved early, because deterioration can be rapid and ventilatory support may be needed.

(c) Simple transfusion raises oxygen-carrying capacity and is appropriate when Hb has fallen, as here, in moderate disease. Hb must not be raised too high, because this increases viscosity and can worsen vaso-occlusion. Exchange transfusion removes sickle cells while giving donor blood, lowering the HbS percentage without raising viscosity. It is used for severe or progressive acute chest syndrome, stroke and multiorgan failure.

(d) Hydroxycarbamide increases HbF and reduces painful crises and acute chest syndrome. Functional hyposplenism requires vaccination and penicillin prophylaxis. Children need transcranial Doppler screening, and those at high stroke risk enter regular transfusion programmes with iron chelation. Stem cell transplantation, or the gene-editing therapy exa-cel authorised by the MHRA in 2023, is an option for selected patients. Education about triggers and psychological support are also important.

questions.q:
Interpret each set of findings, give the most likely diagnosis and outline the key next step in management.

Patient A: Ms Clarke, 34, has lifelong heavy periods and nosebleeds; her mother has similar problems. Platelets normal, PT normal, APTT slightly prolonged.

Patient B: Mr Sharma, 58, is in intensive care with Gram-negative sepsis and is oozing from cannula sites. Platelets low, PT and APTT prolonged, fibrinogen low, D-dimer markedly raised.

Patient C: Mrs Doyle, 63, is 8 days after knee replacement, receiving LMWH. Her platelet count has fallen from 260 to 95 × 10⁹/L, and she has a new swollen calf with a confirmed DVT.

Patient D: Ms Roberts, 31, has had three first-trimester miscarriages. APTT is prolonged and does not correct on mixing with normal plasma.
markScheme: A: mucocutaneous bleeding with autosomal dominant pattern, normal platelets, mildly prolonged APTT (low factor VIII): von Willebrand disease (likely type 1).

A next steps: vWF antigen, vWF activity (platelet-binding assay) and factor VIII levels, blood group consideration; manage with tranexamic acid, hormonal therapy for menorrhagia, desmopressin (after a trial) or vWF concentrate for surgery.
B: consumption of platelets and factors with fibrinolysis: disseminated intravascular coagulation secondary to sepsis.

B next steps: treat the cause (antibiotics, source control, resuscitation); blood products (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen) for active bleeding or procedures, not to correct numbers alone.
C: platelet fall of more than 50%, 5–10 days after heparin, with new thrombosis: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; high 4Ts score.

C next steps: stop all heparin (including flushes), start a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g. argatroban or a suitable alternative per haematology advice), send anti-PF4/heparin antibodies; avoid platelet transfusion; record as heparin allergy.
D: APTT prolonged and not correcting on mixing indicates an inhibitor; with recurrent miscarriage, lupus anticoagulant and antiphospholipid syndrome.

D next steps: confirm with lupus anticoagulant testing plus anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated at least 12 weeks apart; specialist obstetric/haematology care (aspirin and heparin in future pregnancy).
Explains the general principle that APTT prolongation with an inhibitor can coexist with thrombotic, not bleeding, tendency.
Clear structure and correct interpretation of each test.
questions.modelAnswer:
Patient A has lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding, an affected mother, a normal platelet count and a slightly prolonged APTT. This suggests von Willebrand disease, most likely type 1, the commonest inherited bleeding disorder. Low vWF reduces the stability of factor VIII, which explains the APTT. She needs vWF antigen, vWF activity (platelet-binding) and factor VIII levels, interpreted with her blood group in mind, because group O lowers vWF. Menorrhagia can be managed with tranexamic acid or hormonal therapy. Desmopressin, after a test of response, or vWF-containing concentrate covers surgery.

Patient B has low platelets, prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen and a very high D-dimer in sepsis. This is disseminated intravascular coagulation, with widespread activation consuming platelets and factors alongside fibrinolysis. The priority is treating the sepsis with antibiotics, source control and resuscitation. Platelets, fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate are given for bleeding or before procedures, not to correct numbers alone.

Patient C's platelet count has fallen by more than half, 5–10 days after starting LMWH, with a new DVT. That gives a high 4Ts score for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Antibodies against PF4–heparin complexes activate platelets, causing thrombosis. All heparin, including flushes, must be stopped and a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban started on haematology advice. Anti-PF4 antibodies should be sent, platelet transfusion avoided, and the reaction recorded as an allergy.

Patient D has a prolonged APTT that does not correct on mixing, indicating an inhibitor. With recurrent early miscarriage, this suggests lupus anticoagulant and antiphospholipid syndrome. The antibody prolongs phospholipid-dependent tests in the laboratory but promotes thrombosis in the body. Diagnosis requires lupus anticoagulant testing plus anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, persistent on repeat testing at least 12 weeks apart. Future pregnancies need joint obstetric and haematology care, usually with aspirin and heparin.

questions.q:
Mr Harding, a 71-year-old retired teacher, has 3 months of back pain, fatigue and two chest infections. Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, adjusted calcium 3.0 mmol/L, creatinine 210 µmol/L (normal a year ago), total protein raised with low albumin, and ESR markedly raised. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG kappa paraprotein of 42 g/L with suppressed background immunoglobulins. Whole-body low-dose CT shows multiple lytic lesions, and marrow examination shows 35% clonal plasma cells.

(a) Does he meet diagnostic criteria for myeloma? Justify your answer. (b) Explain the mechanisms behind each CRAB feature and his recurrent infections. (c) Outline his immediate management. (d) Summarise the principles of disease-directed treatment.
markScheme: IMWG 2014: clonal marrow plasma cells at least 10% (35%) plus at least one myeloma-defining event; he has all CRAB features, so meets criteria for symptomatic multiple myeloma.
Hypercalcaemia and bone lesions: myeloma cells increase RANKL and reduce OPG, activating osteoclasts, while inhibiting osteoblasts (e.g. via DKK1), so lesions are purely lytic.
Renal impairment: light-chain cast nephropathy, plus hypercalcaemia, dehydration, infection and nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, contrast).
Anaemia: marrow infiltration and inflammatory cytokines (and renal impairment reducing EPO).
Infections: immunoparesis (suppressed normal immunoglobulins), plus neutropenia from marrow infiltration or treatment.
Immediate: IV fluids for hypercalcaemia and AKI; bisphosphonate (adjusted for renal function) or alternative once rehydrated; avoid NSAIDs and nephrotoxins; treat infection.
Assess for spinal cord compression (back pain plus neurology needs urgent MRI); analgesia; consider vertebral fracture management.
Urgent haematology referral; check serum free light chains, β2-microglobulin, LDH, cytogenetics for staging and risk (R-ISS).

Disease-directed treatment: combinations including a proteasome inhibitor (bortezomib), immunomodulatory drug (lenalidomide or thalidomide), corticosteroid (dexamethasone) and anti-CD38 antibody (daratumumab).

Autologous stem cell transplantation for fit patients (fitness, not age alone); supportive care (VTE prophylaxis with immunomodulatory drugs, antiviral/antibacterial prophylaxis, vaccinations); disease remains largely incurable with relapses treated with further lines, including CAR-T or bispecific antibodies.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Yes. The IMWG 2014 criteria need clonal marrow plasma cells of at least 10%, or a plasmacytoma, plus a myeloma-defining event. He has 35% clonal plasma cells and every CRAB feature: hypercalcaemia, new renal impairment, anaemia and lytic bone lesions. This is symptomatic multiple myeloma.

(b) Myeloma cells increase osteoblast RANKL and reduce osteoprotegerin, driving osteoclast activity. At the same time they suppress osteoblasts, partly through DKK1. Bone loss is therefore purely lytic, releasing calcium, which is why isotope bone scans and ALP are often unrevealing. Renal impairment mainly reflects light-chain cast nephropathy, worsened by hypercalcaemia, dehydration, infection and nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs. Anaemia results from marrow infiltration, inflammatory cytokines and reduced erythropoietin from the damaged kidneys. Recurrent infection reflects immunoparesis: the clone suppresses normal immunoglobulin production, impairing antibody responses.

(c) He needs intravenous fluids to correct dehydration, lower calcium and support renal function. Once he is rehydrated, an intravenous bisphosphonate adjusted for renal function treats hypercalcaemia and reduces skeletal events, with dental review because of jaw osteonecrosis risk. NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins should be avoided and infection treated promptly. Back pain in myeloma requires vigilance for spinal cord compression, and any neurological symptoms warrant urgent MRI. Refer urgently to haematology. Serum free light chains, β2-microglobulin, LDH and cytogenetics are needed for staging (R-ISS) and risk assessment.

(d) Initial therapy combines drugs with different mechanisms. Typical classes are a proteasome inhibitor such as bortezomib, an immunomodulatory drug such as lenalidomide, dexamethasone and an anti-CD38 antibody such as daratumumab. Fit patients, judged on fitness rather than age alone, may proceed to autologous stem cell transplantation. Supportive care includes VTE prophylaxis with immunomodulatory drugs, infection prophylaxis and vaccination. Myeloma remains largely incurable, so relapses are treated with further lines, including CAR-T cells and bispecific antibodies.

questions.q: "Chronic myeloid leukaemia and acute promyelocytic leukaemia show that targeted therapy can transform haematological malignancy, but they are exceptions rather than the rule." Discuss.
markScheme: CML: t(9;22) BCR::ABL1 is a single dominant driver tyrosine kinase; imatinib binds the ATP-binding site and blocks signalling.
IRIS trial (2003): imatinib superior to interferon plus cytarabine; long-term follow-up shows survival approaching that of the general population for many patients.

Resistance mechanisms (kinase domain mutations, e.g. T315I) addressed by later TKIs (ponatinib; asciminib, an allosteric STAMP inhibitor); treatment-free remission possible for some with sustained deep molecular response.

APL: PML::RARA blocks differentiation; ATRA induces differentiation and arsenic trioxide promotes PML::RARA degradation; APL0406 (Lo-Coco et al., 2013) showed ATRA plus arsenic at least as effective as ATRA plus chemotherapy in non-high-risk APL; differentiation syndrome is a key toxicity.
Other successes: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib, RESONATE 2014) and the BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax in CLL; rituximab in B-cell lymphoma; CAR-T cells and bispecific antibodies in lymphoma, ALL and myeloma.
Why exceptions: CML and APL have a single initiating fusion oncoprotein in a relatively genetically stable clone; most malignancies (AML, myeloma) are genetically heterogeneous with clonal evolution.
AML: targeted agents (FLT3 inhibitor midostaurin in RATIFY, 2017; IDH inhibitors) improve outcomes modestly in subsets, but cure rates in older adults remain low.
Myeloma and CLL: targeted therapies extend survival but are rarely curative; continuous therapy, cost and toxicity (CRS, ICANS with CAR-T) are issues.
Even in CML, therapy usually suppresses rather than eradicates leukaemic stem cells; adherence and long-term toxicity matter.
Balanced conclusion: the paradigm has spread but complete transformation depends on a dominant, druggable driver.
questions.modelAnswer:
Chronic myeloid leukaemia is driven by the BCR::ABL1 fusion produced by t(9;22), a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. Imatinib occupies its ATP-binding site and shuts down downstream signalling. In the IRIS trial (2003), imatinib outperformed interferon with cytarabine, and long-term follow-up shows many patients now have near-normal life expectancy. Resistance, often from kinase domain mutations such as T315I, has been met by later inhibitors including ponatinib and the allosteric agent asciminib. Some patients with sustained deep molecular responses can stop therapy altogether. In acute promyelocytic leukaemia, the PML::RARA fusion blocks myeloid differentiation. All-trans retinoic acid releases the block and arsenic trioxide degrades the fusion protein. APL0406 (Lo-Coco and colleagues, 2013) showed this chemotherapy-free combination was at least as effective as ATRA with chemotherapy in non-high-risk disease. A once rapidly fatal leukaemia became highly curable.

These successes share a feature: one initiating fusion oncoprotein on which the clone depends, in a relatively genetically stable disease. Most haematological cancers lack this. AML is genetically heterogeneous and evolves under treatment. FLT3 inhibition with midostaurin (RATIFY, 2017) and IDH inhibitors help defined subsets, but cure rates in older adults remain poor. In CLL, BTK inhibitors (RESONATE, 2014) and venetoclax have largely replaced chemoimmunotherapy and transformed survival, especially in TP53-disrupted disease, yet they rarely cure and often require continuous therapy. Myeloma survival has improved greatly with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, anti-CD38 antibodies, CAR-T cells and bispecifics, but relapse is almost universal.

Even CML is not fully solved: leukaemic stem cells persist, so most patients stay on lifelong therapy, with issues of adherence, cost and toxicity. Immunotherapies broaden the targeted approach but add toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity.

In conclusion, the statement is largely right. CML and APL remain the clearest transformations because each has a dominant, druggable driver. The targeted principle has nevertheless spread widely, turning several fatal diseases into chronic ones, even where cure remains elusive.
